The house resumed from February 10 consideration in committee on Bill No. 7 to amend the Patent Act. Mr. Rinfret. Mr. Johnston in the chair:
On section 1-Manufacture for reasonable requirements.

When we were discussing thfg
section the other day reference was made to the words:
Not less than one year after the thirteenth day of June one thousand nine hundred and twenty-three.
It was pointed out quite properly that this revision was perfectly obsolete. I may say that it was intended in this act to reproduce the exact wording of the revised statutes. I quite admit it has no meaning at all. At the same time, if we adopt the other phrase, "one year after the passing of this act" it may be misconstrued, and may be interpreted to mean that we intend to give an additional year to the holder of the patent. I move that we rescind the amendment made the other day, and strike out the words: "and not less than one year after the thirteenth day of June one thousand nine hundred and twenty-three."

Will the minister tell me what he proposes to do, now that he has struck out the amendment, in regard to having in Canada a national patent and trade mark policy? On looking up the records I find that under this section over 90 per cent of the trade marks are owned by aliens. My
point is that all these patents which deal with the raw materials or natural resources of Canada should be under the control of Canadians. The commissioner of patents should be given power to require that these patents shall stay in Canada and that the product shall be manufactured in Canada for the time limit of one year. I find in other countries where similar legislation is in force, what they call a national policy, and provision is made for the revocation of a patent in such cases. What is the result to-day of this patent law which we have in Canada? Has there been any revocation?
I do not believe there has been a single revocation. An American citizen comes into Canada, goes to the patent office and files his application under this section or some other section. He procures his patent, goes to the United States with the patent in his pocket, takes the raw material from Canada and manufactures it in the United States.
In the case of the radio and motor car business, if we had a law providing that all the work should be done in Canada, it would create employment for our people. You cannot go to Washington and secure a patent, and then take the profits accruing therefrom out of the country, for there they have a national policy in the patent office, a policy that applies also in other departments of the United States government. To-day we have no brakes to control patentees, and I am confident that a return to the house will show that over ninety per cent of our patents and trademarks are held by other than British subjects. If this bill is the best the government can do in consolidating our patent act, the sooner we make a patent law after the American pattern the better it will be for Canada.

Mr. Chairman, as I explained the other day, the object of this bill is to bring our patent act into conformity with the decisions arrived at by the countries which met at The Hague international conference. On Friday the committee was quite agreeable to the bill. I think my hon. friend will agree that when a patent is granted we should see to it that within a reasonable time the patentee manufactures under his patent for the benefit of the country.

I would remind the minister that this bill is now before the parliament of Canada, not The Hague conference. I appeal to him as a Canadian interested in the development of our natural resources to see to it that we have in our patent law a national policy that will ensure the patented
Patent Act

article being manufactured in Canada for at least a year, to give Canadians a chance of employment. Our present patent law is driving our people across the border to work up our raw materials there.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When this bill was last before the committee clause 1 was amended. In line 8 the words:
-thirteenth day of June one thousand nine hundred and twenty-threewere stricken out, and the words:
-after the passing of this act substituted. The minister now moves that the amendment be rescinded and the words in the seventh and following lines:
and not less than one year after the thirteenth day of June one thousand nine hundred and twenty-three
be struck out.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.

I now ask, Mr. Chairman, that we revert to clause 2, where the same situation occurs. I move that we also rescind the amendment agreed to last Friday and that the words:
not less than one year after the thirteenth day of June, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-three
be stricken out.
Please read the amendment.
It is the same amendment as we have made in the preceding clause.
Amendment agreed to.

Since the bill was in committee some interested parties have reported to me that we might possibly make a change at the thirty-first line. It says:
if a license in respect of said patent has previously been granted under section 40,
I may explain that the commissioner of patents does not grant the license; he simply orders the patentee to do so. The intention of the legislation would be carried out if we substitute for the word "granted" the word " ordered," because a case might arise where a patentee had been ordered to grant a license and had not done so. I believe that under the other sections of the act we could still proceed against him and revoke his patent. However, I think the clause will be much clearer if it is made to read:
if a license in respect of said patent has previously been ordered under section 40.

I would therefore move, Mr. Chairman, that in line 31 we strike out the word "granted" and insert the word " ordered."
Amendment agreed to.

Mr. Chairman, in the same section, a few lines below the place to which the minister has just referred, are the following words:
and unless the patentee proves that the patented article or process is manufactured or carried on to an adequate extent in Canada.
Will he kindly explain what "adequate extent" means?

A similar question was put to me the other day. It is within the discretion of the commissioner. If my hon. friend will revert to clause 1, subsection (c), he will see that the commissioner considers the petition, and has discretion to determine whether in his judgment the requirements of the public are adequately provided for and the article adequately manufactured. I may say to my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) that although we were very much pleased last week to do away with the split infinitive, the words "adequately manufactured" are used throughout the bill, and practically form a verb by themselves. It is immaterial either way.

Mr. Chairman, I expected some such answer from the minister. I believe the reason why Canadian patents are not as well taken care of as they ought to be is that there is too much power given to the commissioner of patents. You should have your law so framed that if a patent is void, it is void; and if it is not void, then the commissioner should have no discretion.

I welcome my hon. friend's opinion, which I prize very highly. There is no intention in this bill to alter the principle of our patent law. We are merely bringing our legislation into conformity with the decisions of The Hague conference in respect of such minor matters as I have indicated. I shall be only too pleased to consider my hon. friend's representations and if possible make a more extensive study of the whole patent law with a view to its general revision.
I did not catch the full purport of the amendment; perhaps the minister will read it again.

The amendment is very plain. It was provided in the amending act of 1923 that the disposition would obtain for one year, and when the revision was made this was carried into the revised statutes-

Patent Act
"not less than one year after the thirteenth day of June, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-three This is now quite obsolete.
I am sure my hon. friend will have no objection to the amendment in this respect, and the other amendment consists merely in the changing of a word. Subsection 2 empowers the commissioner to consider the application,
" and if a license in respect of said patent has previously been granted under section 40", then certain action is taken. This is what I should call a clerical error, because we do not grant licenses under section 40; we order the license to be granted by the patentee. The only change, therefore, is from the word " granted " to the word " ordered ".

It seems that parliament is being asked to hand over the administration of the act to a commissioner who may or may not grant licenses for political purposes. The word " granted " is changed to " ordered ", Subsection 2 provides for the revocation of the patent unless it is shown to the satisfaction of the commissioner that the patented article or process " is manufactured or carried on within Canada to an adequate extent ", Do these words imply that the applicant for a patent may be at liberty to bring in foreign labour, skilled or unskilled, in violation of our Alien Labour Act, as is actually done now? In the city I come from a number of men were brought in from the south to work in the nursery business, notwithstanding that similar labour could have been obtained in Canada. In my opinion this bill should take account of the provisions of the alien labour law in this respect. Will it not be possible for the holders of patents, under this provision, to bring in skilled and unskilled labour from the United States under the terms of paragraph (b) from which I have quoted?

My hon. friend has repeated the argument he advanced on the previous section and I thought he would take it that I had not changed my view of the matter. We have discussed this question before and it has been pointed out that the proposed legislation is intended to carry out the terms of a mutual agreement on the part of the nations that met at The Hague. It is a plausible argument that this parliament does not sit at The Hague but in Ottawa. That is perfectly true. But is it not desirable that we should take advantage of the protection which will be afforded us by the participating countries? Surely it is not a bad thing now and then to cultivate the international spirit in matters of this kind which 56103-28
link the nations together. Really, to be perfectly frank, I must say that my hon. friend's objection does not appeal to me.

I do not quite appreciate the
object in changing the word "granted" to the word "ordered". I can understand that the license might be ordered, but there comes a time when it is actually issued. Surely, therefore, the intention must be to make it applicable not only to licenses which have been ordered but to licenses which have been issued.

The commissioner orders
the license to be granted but the license is granted by the patentee himself. Of course, under section 40, if he fails to issue the license within a certain time limit we may revoke the patent.	We thought that the
provision would be better worded in the manner now proposed. We order that the patent be granted; that is the only thing we do as a department. The commissioner orders the patentee to grant the license.

Is not the license eventually
issued by the department?

It is granted by the
patentee himself.

But take the document itself,
the license: where does it come from?

It is registered in the
department, but we have no way of compelling tjhe patentee to grant the license. We may, however, revoke his patent. The proposed amendment aims simply at making the provision clearer and bringing it more into harmony with the previous section.

I do not think the minister
grasps my point. What I want to indicate is that there comes a time when the license is issued, and so far as I know it is issued by the department. I may be wrong in that regard; if so-if it is issued by the patentee . -then I agree with the minister.

Under the copyright law, where application is made for a license the department grants it; under the patent law, on the other hand, the department issues the order and the patentee grants the license. If our instructions have not been followed and the license is not granted, then we may proceed under section 40.
Section as amended agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.



St. John and Quebec Railway
The house resumed, from February 10, consideration in committee of Bill No. 8, to amend the Trade Mark and Design Act.- Mr. Rinfret-Mr. Johnston in the chair.

I move that we revert
to section 6.
On section 6-Filing of application already filed in another country.

I have an amendment
which will change the wording of this section. The leader of the opposition pointed out the other day that in the first two lines of that section the words "as enacted by section 3 of chapter 28 of the statutes of 1923," had become obsolete, and my purpose is to move that the section be amended by striking out those words. I also move that the figures 49 at the beginning of the new section be changed to 52. The house resumed, from February 10, consideration in committee of Bill No. 9, to authorize an extension of time for the completion of the St. John and Quebec Railway between Centrevil'le, in the county of Carle-ton, and Andover, in the county of Victoria, N.B.-Mr. Dunning-Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-extension of time.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals): The other day, when this bill was before the committee, the leader of (he opposition called my attention to a point in connection with it, and the bill was left in committee in order that I might have the opportunity to (take the matter up again with the Department of Justice. I have done so. and the Department of Justice regards the amendment in its present form as quite sufficient for the purpose, and I am also advised that the Premier of New Brunswick, who is really the promoter of the line in question, is perfectly satisfied with it as it now appears, and he requests it in this form.

I have been a member
of the railway committee for six years, and I (Mr. Rinfret.J
have never known a bill asking for an extension of time which has not been referred to that committee. I do not see why any exception should be made even in this case of a government bill. We have a committee appointed by this house to deal with questions of charters and extensions of time and so on, and I am going to move that this bill be referred to the select standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

Probably my hon. friend was not present the other day when this matter was referred to the committee of the whole instead of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, as is usually the case. The reason for dealing with it in this manner is that this is not an ordinary railway charter; the railway in question is owned by the government of the province of New Brunswick, and the extension is asked for by that government. It was therefore thought quite proper to deal with it in this way, as no private interests are involved in any sense and it is not necessary to call witnesses and go through the usual procedure. I should also say that this railway is in operation already, and this extension refers to a branch which is not yet constructed.

Technically the minister
may be correct, and this may only be one exception, but at the same time I see no reason why the house should be asked to deal with railway bills in this w-ay. The predecessor of the present minister had all the branch line bills, government and private, sent to the railway committee, for consideration, and even the estimates of the Canadian National Railways are sent to a committee of this house to be dealt with. All the branch line bibs were sent to the railway committee, and that is the only regular way in which bills of this kind should be considered under the rules of the house. Some of these companies are only paper companies; they get a charter and then ask for repeated extensions of time. We had two or three bills before the railway committee during the last two or three sessions requesting an extension of time, and hardly a dollar had been spent on any of them. I contend that this process violates the whole principle of the Railway Act. For these reasons I think the minister should agree to have this bill dealt with in the regular way.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Royal Military College
The house resumed from February 10, consideration in committee of Bill No. 13, respecting the Royal Military College of Canada-Mr. Ralston.-Mr. Johnston in the chair.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
When the bill was last under
consideration section 7 was allowed to stand, and also section 9. In. reference to section 7 the committee will remember we were discussing the provisions for the admission of cadets to the college. As I pointed out, the provision which was retained in the old act was obsolete because of the fact that now there is no preliminary examination; the examinations are based on standards of educational qualifications in the different provinces, and it was unworkable to select candidates from the whole of the Dominion in order of merit. I have, however, considered the suggestions which were made at that time to incorporate as far as possible the principle of merit, and, as I indicated to the committee, whether it is incorporated in the act by regulation or practice, it is the only standard under which the act will be administered. I now suggest to the committee that the following words be inserted at the beginning of section 7:
The selection of cadets from each province shall be in order of merit, and
This I think will be found satisfactory. The reason the words "from each province" are inserted is because it is felt we cannot put together all the candidates from the Dominion and simply select them in order of merit. That would not be fair to the individual provinces and would not give them their quota.

I should like to see a
change made in the law with respect to this splendid institution under which the period for obtaining a diploma would be changed from four to three years where it was for over thirty-five years until recently. A complaint I hear made in respect to the Royal Military College is in regard to matriculation or entrance. In every province there is a separate examination for matriculation, and I think that the change made in the system followed at Kingston has not been in the best interests of that institution. We should go back to the old system and let the college run its own entrance.
I should like to quote from a letter written to me at my request by Mr. Iva E. Martin, M.A., who was director of studies at the college for many years, and is now one of 56103-28J
my constituents. Mr. Martin was one of the most brilliant students in mathematics who ever graduated from Toronto university, and was a most efficient and successful member of the staff of the Royal Military College for over thirty years. The minister should see to it that in the matter of literary requirements the college should go forward and not backward. Merit alone should be the test of entrance with one examination for all.
May I be permitted to read two or three paragraphs of the letter in question? Professor Martin has the confidence of all classes of graduates. He did more to make the college than anyone else. He says:
This proposed act will put into a practical form the authority necessary to continue the institution as it is nowr being conducted. The old act has been out of date for years. Regulations issued from time to time by the governor in council is the real basis of its operations and this act merely authorizes this constitution.
I would suggest that paragraph 2 (1) of the proposed act be made to read something as follows:
2. (I) There shall be an institution for the purpose of imparting a preliminary education in military subjects such as tactics, fortification, engineering, etc., and a general introduction to such scientific subjects as may be connected with, and necessary to, the technical education of a military officer in the performance of his duties in the military profession. Also for qualifying officers for command and for staff appointments.
Paragraph 5 indicates the "qualifications" of the commandant which are difficult of realization in the practice, and I think that he should be "assisted" by a director of studies who should be selected from the civil members of his staff.
Professor Martin is right in all he says. There should be a director of studies under the commandant with increased duties and powers. I hope the minister will see his way clear to provide improved buildings, equipment and grounds and a recreation hall for the Royal Military College so that it may not lag behind McGill. Queens and other universities and colleges, and grant better pay to the staff and give them quarters at less rates.

Before the amendment
carries I should like to say that the clause appears to me to be very indefinite. No one can say how "order of merit" is to be determined. Merit in what? In athletics, in scholarships, in Sunday school work?

Merit in the subjects
required for the examination.

The clause does not say so. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this matter is left entirely at large without any definition, it may be purely guess work. Anyone can come later on and say merit is one thing,
Royal Military College

and somebody else will say it is another thing, and the point will be decided according to the decision of the commandant or the minister.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.

Regarding clause 9 the
suggestion was made that the old act provided a limitation of the amount to be paid by each student. I have incorporated that in an amended section which I will read to the committee:
9. Every cadet shall be required to furnish himself with such books, apparatus and equipment as are not supplied by the college, and to pay a sum not exceeding the rate of $300 per annum and such allowances as are from time to time authorized by the governor in council to meet the ordinary expenses of living and the procuring of uniform.
Do I understand that the student will have to pay for his tuition and board the amount of $300 per annum? .

I have sent down for a
statement as to just what it does include. I can only assure my hon. friend that this is exactly the provision that is in the old act. The cadet will not have to pay any more under this bill than under the old act. I gave the figures when we were considering this bill before, to the effect that they only paid $300 per year, except the first year when they paid $550, $250 being allowance for uniform.

What I am going to say may not be very popular, but that will not be an unusual experience with me in this house. Needless to say* I have a great admiration for the Royal Military College, for the work it is doing and for the reputation which its graduates have made throughout the world. I am not sure that we are on the right track in limiting t'he cost to what it has been in the past, namely, $300. The cost of obtaining a degree in arts, medicine or science in any of our Canadian universities is far below the cost of the education provided to a cadet of the Royal Military College. In so far as we limit the cost to the student, we increase the cost to the country, provided that we increase the accommodation at the college for a greater number of students- It may be advisable to keep the expenditure down to about where it is or where it has been; but if we are to do that and at the same time increase the accommodation so that more students can attend-and I think that should be done-it seems to me that it is about time

and very proper that we should consider whether or not the cost borne by the students might not be increased to a certain degree. I am not going to suggest what that cost should be; but the very fact that that sum of $300 has obtained for so many years, notwithstanding what we all know to be the fact that the cost of education in all other institutions has enormously increased in comparison with what it was a number of years ago, suggests that the matter of what the students should pay, without too large a burden being placed upon them, is one which might very fairly be considered from the standpoint of fair play to all concerned.
The Royal Military College is regarded, and rightly so, as giving a very efficient and select education to carefully selected men from all parts of Canada. The cost to the student is very low as compared with that of other institutions such as universities. I should like to see the number of students increased. That, of course, would mean an increase in the cost to the country unless some appreciable increase in cost was placed upon the student himself. I may not be on a popular line in expressing the thought that the student should pay more money; but having regard to all the circumstances and changed conditions, I submit it is a matter which is worthy of our careful consideration.

There are perhaps many
of us who on general principles would feel inclined to concur in what my hon. friend has said; but in amending this act I have felt that-1 do not want to introduce any new principle. The point is that the accommodation has not been increased, and when the accommodation is increased I quite agree with him that it may be well for whoever is considering the matter to consider an increase of charge to the student as well. I should like the committee to remember that these students are selected in a different way from students going to an ordinary educational institution. In every other institution the doors are wide open to students. Before a student obtains the privilege, for it is a privilege, of receiving this education in the Royal Military College, he must show a certain qualification, a certain aptness, a certain physical fitness, a certain mental alertness, and, in short, he must measure up to a certain standard. Therefore it is felt that it is perhaps not advisable at this stage, when I am merely suggesting more or less formal amendments to the act for the purpose of bringing it up to date, that we should consider increasing the cost to the student. When the

Canteen Funds
accommodation becomes more luxurious and extensive, there may be an opportunity for considering that matter.

I quite appreciate the viewpoint of the minister and I am prepared to concur in it. Has he under his hand sufficient material to enable him to inform the committee what percentage of the graduates of the Royal Military College follow a military career after leaving the college?

I do not have that just
under my hand. Speaking from memory I would think those who actually enter the permanent forces are less than five per cent, but I would also point out that in the late war ninety-nine per cent of the living students who were physically fit took their part and behaved themselves creditably as students of the Royal Military College should do.

Might I ask the minister if the supplies are going to be purchased under the federal patronage system? With the increased fees and the uniform and equipment required, the Royal Military College is now looked upon as a rich man's college. 'Nowadays out of sixteen collegiate institutes in the Toronto district the college does not get more than one or two students a year, while in other years it got quite a number. There is no other institution in Canada where there is more party patronage as regards not only the staff, civil and military, and the help, but the purchase of the equipment, repairs to buildings, new buildings and supplies. They even built a road through the constituency of the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) under the patronage system, and he can tell how at great expense a little bit of macadam and concrete road was built some of it without tender, which could have been put in by any city engineer for one-third of the cost. The whole tendency seems to turn this institution from what it was intended by its founders into a rich man's college. The course has been lengthened to four years; the fees have been increased as well as the equipment and supplies. The whole thing is just a patronage institution for the benefit of the Liberal party in the city of Kingston and in the county of Frontenac. All the supplies are being bought down there. If the department would buy the text books in the same way as the largeT boards of education in Canada do, they would save this institution and the cadets from one-quarter to one-third of the present cost. I should like the minister to consider the policy of buying these books and supplying them
to the students, charging so much for them and thus effecting an economy.

If my hon. friend knows of any instances in connection with which any improper expenditures have been made, I trust he will bring the matter to my attention when the estimates of the Royal Military College are before the house. As regards patronage I want to say to him that I know of no institution under any government department that is conducted as free from party patronage as this institution is, and while I happen to hold the position I do, that condition of things will remain, because I do not propose to have this institution made anything other than what it is, namely, a place where deserving young men, men who will become creditable Canadians will be able to obtain an education at a moderate cost and thus be fitted to take their part in their country's affairs.
I hope the day is far distant when, as was suggested on a former occasion in this house, the present Postmaster-General (Mr. Yeniot) might succeed the Minister of National Defence.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to provide for the disposition and allotment of the canteen funds which were accumulated during the war by certain units of the Canadian expeditionary force in Canada, the Canadian Siberian forces and by the forces stationed at St. Lucia (British West Indies), resulting from the profits of canteens and other like institutions operated by the several units and formations, and for the administration of the same by the provincial! board of trustees appointed under the Canteen Funds Act. chapter 34 of the statutes of 1925.
Motion agreed to, and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
Perhaps the minister will make a statement.

There is deposited with
the Receiver General of Canada the sum of about $124,000 which has been accumulated from the profits of canteens operated by units which have their local organizations in Canada, which did not themselves proceed overseas. These were units such as depot detachments, hospital units and things of that sort, and in
Canteen Funds

addition to that there were three units not so localized such as the Siberian expeditionary force, the St. Lucia forces, and the Y.M.C.A., all of which accumulated profits, and these had been paid to the receiver general.

About what do they
amount to?
That is what is left?

Yes. The way in which it is proposed to dispose of these funds-we are advised that it is necessary to enact legislation-is to divide it up into allotments according to provinces and hand the funds over to the canteen boards which were constituted under the act of 1925. The administration will naturally be somewhat different, and the proportions to the provinces will be somewhat different from the overseas canteen funds, but that is a matter rvhich I think can be taken care of by the provincial boards when the moneys come to their hands. What we have done is this: we have taken the place of organization of a particular depot unit, and have allotted the funds, the profits of that unit, to the particular province where the organization took place. Generally speaking the enlistments were made from a province in which the unit was situated. In addition to that we have the Siberian forces, the St. Lucia forces, and the Y.M.C.A. force, and in this case the division proposed is according to the enlistments in each province. By a combination of the two a percentage has been made up which is given in the schedule to the bill based on this resolution, and it is proposed to hand the funds over in these proportions to the various provinces- I do not know whether the committee will be interested in having the percentages given or not. I will give the figures roughly, leaving out the second decimal. They are as follows:
Per cent
Alberta	 6.5
British Columbia	 3.6
Manitoba	 10.9
New Brunswick	 5.5
Nova Scotia	 4.1
Ontario	 41.5
Prince Edward Island	32
Quebec	 23.5
Saskatchewan	 3.1

Can the minister give
it in dollars and cents?

May I ask if this scheme
which is now propounded has been approved by the Canadian Legion and the other soldier organizations?

I cannot say at the
moment. The officers of my department were in consultation with some of these representatives, but I cannot answer offhand.

Are those funds being
divided up on the same basis as the other funds of last year, and by the same organization? I think I understood the minister to say they were.

They are being divided
by thS same organization and on the same basis, except that my hon. friend must remember that those who were overseas would probably not expect to share in those funds, because those who originally enlisted in the depot units and went overseas are supposed to have gotten the benefits of the profits from the depot canteens when they sailed. Conducting officeis were given a certain amount for comforts, which was supposed to represent in theory at least a. fair proportion of the unexpended profits up to that time. So that those who will share in this fund, will be largely those who have not gone overseas, and who have not derived any benefit from any other source.

No. I shall be glad to
have any suggestions because we all recog-, nize that we are to some extent dealing with

Canteen Funds
a fund which, in the strict legal interpretation at least, may belong to individuals, but which in a lump sum will permit something tangible being done with it. Therefore any helpful suggestions I shall be very glad to have.

Were not these funds
accumulated from the money of men who were overseas?

These funds particularly
were not. I think, accumulated from men who were overseas. As I tried to point out, those who went overseas, in theory at least, and, 1 think they will agree, generally in practice too, received the benefit of the profits of the depot canteens from which they made their purchases. Then those who were overseas began to get the benefit of canteen funds from overseas canteens, but those who remained in Canada still kept contributing to those depot canteen funds, and it i- they and their dependants who, I think, would benefit largely by any disposition of these funds. The bill to follow this resolution does provide that any use of the provincial allotment for relief purposes should be limited to the class of case for which no relief is then available from governmental sources* or from the allotment made under the Canteen Funds Act. In other words, it proposes to provide for the class of men who contributed most generally towards the funds still left.

Mr. Chairman, I think the
minister ought to be able to assure the committee generally that those men who did go overseas and did contribute to these funds actually received the proportion to which they were entitled. I have grave doubts that that is the fact. I do not think it was the custom to pay them tbi exact proportion of the funds to which they would have been entitled had a division been made at the time. True, they may have been given something from the funds when they went overseas, but I do not think it is generally accepted that they received the proportion to which they would have been actually entitled if the funds had been divided at the time. Therefore I do not think the men who went overseas should entirely be disentitled to something from these funds.

I endeavoured to make
it clear to the committee that I thought in theory at least-that is the word I used- these men were supposed to have received the benefit of the funds that had accumulated; but there was no accounting, and there may have been more contributed than was paid out. We have to deal with the practical
situation here and the question is whether it is worth while attempting to divide the small amount of money among all the men who contributed, or to confine it to those who were members of the depot units. As I said to my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion) a few moments ago, I shall be very glad to receive suggestions from the committee when the bill is under consideration. The principal thought in mind is not to dissipate the money so that it will not do any good.

What information has the
government secured from those directly interested in the funds? After all, their representations should have some bearing on the disposition of the money.

I cannot give my hon.
friend an answer in regard to this particular resolution, I can only speak of the representations which were made to the commission which considered canteen funds generally two or three years ago. At that time it was represented that these funds should not be divided among individuals, but should be used for the relief and general benefit of those most in need. That is the principle which I think our ex-service men would like to see carried out, and it is the principle under which the provincial boards are administering the funds received from overseas canteens.
Why were they not included at the time?
This particular fund was not the immediate subject of the investigation to which I refer, although that investigation had to do with similar funds accumulated overseas.
Has the minister any information as to the amount received from each of the sources outlined, for instance, the Siberian forces, the forces stationed at St. Lucia, and so on?

I could give my hon. friend the proportions going to the different provinces from these funds. I do not se-em to have under my hand the total received from the Siberian forces. This is. to amend the section which provides that the court may adjourn any session from time to time and meet again, at the time appointed, for the transaction of business. speechtext:
Hon. FERNAND RINFRET (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of Bill No. 33, to amend the public printing and stationery act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-How expenses shall be met.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OP ACT RESPECTING ADVANCES TO THE KING'S PRINTER
speechtext:
I expressed the opinion
the other day that this bill was an endeavour

Printing and Stationery Act
to place a limitation on the working capital of the department in the sum of $700,000, but I pointed out that the last words of the measure were intended to place unlimited discretion in the power of the governor in council and for that reason were most objectionable. It will be observed that the working capital of the department may by this section be increased up to a sum not to exceed $700,000. If the bill stopped there it would be easily understood. But these words follow:
Or such sum as may hereafter be determined, from time to time, by the governor in council.
It is perfectly obvious that you cannot in one sentence place a limitation of the amount and then, in another sentence, use language that places no limitation on the sum that may be granted by the governor in council. Here we have a parliamentary restriction to $700,000 and at the same time a parliamentary grant to the governor in council of power to increase that sum to any extent in the world. That, I submit, should not be done and cannot possibly be in the mind of the minister. You cannot restrict with one hand and with the other confer unlimited power.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OP ACT RESPECTING ADVANCES TO THE KING'S PRINTER
speechtext:
There is much force in
my hon. friend's argument and I am quite willing to meet his views in that respect. The idea behind the legislation was to rectify a situation which has existed for some time. While the statute provided for an advance to the printing bureau of $200,000 at a time, it happened that the advances were liable to be protracted according to special circumstances. The object was to increase the limit to $700,000 and also to provide for a possible emergency, if that amount should prove insufficient, as for instance in the event of a long recess where no estimates were voted. I quite agree with my hon. friend that there is a contradiction in fixing a limitation and at the same time providing that there be none. I move, therefore, that the section as it stands be amended by striking out the words "or such sum as may hereafter be determined, from time to time, by the governor in council." I may add, however, that it is just possible that this will afford the minister occasion to come back in future sessions with similar bills.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OP ACT RESPECTING ADVANCES TO THE KING'S PRINTER
speechtext:
The minister appreciated the point the other day and I assure him that I appreciate his position. But may I suggest to him, as being in charge of the Printing and Stationery department, that when he mentioned the other day the fact that he had inventories amounting to half
a million dollars he might have reflected that it is sound business in these days to keep inventories as low as possible. I was amazed to find that his inventories totalled that sum, while he was asking for a working capital of $700,000. If he has read the book recently published by Mr. Ford he will see that when that gentleman was confronted with a difficult situation he saw the wisdom of reducing inventories. And .with the paper business, of all businesses in the world, it is highly desirable to keep inventories as low as possible, or a loss will be suffered.

Agriculture-dairying, including grant of $5,000 to the National Dairy Council, $265,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
The committee will notice that there is not very much change in the size of this vote; the $14,000 increase is largely accounted for by salary increases which came into effect last year. There are three or four main items ;into which this sum is divided; part of it is taken up with research
Supply-Agricult ure

work, part with the grading of butter throughout the country and a part is spent on educational work. I will give the details as soon as I get the figures, which will be here in a moment.
The minister mentioned the grading of butter. I would like to ask if there is now a standard system of grading butter in the Dominion?

The grading is uniform now. The western provinces formerly did their own grading and we accepted their grades, but that was found to be not very satisfactory. They wanted to include more in their grading than was the case in the east, so an arrangement was made about a year ago whereby we would take over the grading for all the western provinces, and that is what was done.
Does that grading only apply to butter for export, or to butter for domestic use as well?

It is only for export, although the same grades are used for domestic butter. Tor home consumption the grading is only voluntary, while for export it is compulsory. The export business, of course, has now come to be very small.

As the minister very properly says, the exports of butter have come to be very small, and there are very good reasons why that condition has come about, some of which I desire to place before the minister for his most careful and prayerful consideration. For two or three moments I would like to refer to the effect of the foolish legislation put through in 1925 upon the dairying interests in Canada when this government entered into an agreement with Australia and New Zealand. That trade agreement came into force with regard to Australia on October 1, 1925, and was extended by order in council to New Zealand. At the time that agreement was made the rates of duty on butter under the tariff of 1907 were 4 cents general and intermediate, and 3 cents British preferential. Under the Paterson plan operating in Australia three cents a pound on every pound of butter manufactured in the commonwealth was put into a pool, and out of that pool six cents a pound was paid on each pound of butter exported. This, it is quite obvious, has given a very decided advantage to the producers of butter in Australia, apart altogether from the climatic advantages that they enjoy, over the producers of butter in Canada. New Zealand and Australian butter can be shipped from those countries to Van-

couver for slightly less than 3 cents a pound; I think I am correct in that statement. Now let us see how that works out. Suppose every pound of butter shipped from Australia has cost the producer the extra 3 cents a pound that goes into the pool. Well, he receives a bonus of 6 cents, so that he has sufficient left over, after paying the 3 cents into the pool, to carry his butter to Vancouver without costing him a cent-at least he comes into competition with the producer in Vancouver under as little handicap as if Australia were only a short distance away. There is another advantage given to him. Australian and New Zealand butter arrive at Vancouver and can be shipped from there to Montreal for $2.30 per hundred pounds. Add to that a cent a pound for the duty now imposed and you get S3.30 per hundred pounds. But suppose the producer in British Columbia wants to send a carload of butter to Montreal. In that case the freight rate on his butter from Vancouver to Montreal will be $3.58i per hundred pounds. In other words he is at a disadvantage, as compared with the Australian and New Zealand producer, of 28jf cents per hundred pounds in competing in the market in Montreal. New Zealand butter imported into Vancouver in November, December and January last was laid down there at 34 cents a pound all charges paid. That meant that butter produced in Saskatchewan and shipped from Regina or Saskatoon to Vancouver had to be sold in carload lots at 31i cents, for the reason that it cost 2i cents a pound to send that butter from the points named to Vancouver. The price therefore, as I say, was fixed by the importations in the province of Saskatchewan.
Another point to which I wish to draw attention is this: There is a spread between the winter and summer price of milk right here in Ontario and Quebec. In this city it amounts to 40 cents, and in Montreal to 90 cents per hundred pounds. In Montreal the summer price is, I think, $2 per hundred pounds, and the winter price $2.90. Surely it must be obvious to every person who notes that difference in the cost of producing milk in summer as compared with the cost of production in winter, how very unfair it is that the producers in Canada, with a climate such as we have, should be forced to compete with those who have no winter and enjoy summer weather the year round.
Let us see for a moment the effect of this on the western provinces. Take first the province of Saskatchewan. In 1900 that province produced only 339 pounds of butter. There was then no such thing as a dairy industry in Saskatchewan. In 1910 it produced 1,548,000

Supply-Agriculture
pounds; in 1925,	15,946,000 pounds; in
1926,	16,629,000 pounds. Well, you may
say, notwithstanding the conclusion of the agreement with Australia in October, 1925, the production in Saskatchewan in 1926 was greater than in the previous year. That is very true, but the effect from the importations, which was bound to occur later, had not then been felt. In other words you would not expect every farmer in Saskatchewan to knock every one of his cows on the head immediately after the agreement came into effect, but as soon as the Saskatchewan producers began to feel the effect of this trade arrangement they began to go out of the dairy business. For instance, compare the production in Saskatchewan for the first ten months of 1926 of 15,730,000 pounds with the production in the same ten months of 1927 of 11,502,000 pounds, a reduction of over 4.000,000 pounds, or a decrease of 26.8 per cent. In the month of October, 1925 the production in Saskatchewan amounted to 1,302,432 pounds, whereas in the same month of 1927 it dropped to 633,062 pounds, a decrease of 48.6 per cent. At the present time Saskatchewan is making about 50,000 pounds of butter a week and consuming about 200,000 pounds in the same period. Why should not those extra
150,000	pounds be made by the farmers of Saskatchewan instead of buying it from the farmers of Australia and New Zealand? On undoubted information twenty butter factories which had been in operation in Saskatchewan for years went out of business in the month of November last year, and went out of business for good.
The same story is told with regard to the effect of this trade arrangement on the butter industry in Alberta. The decrease in production in each of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta in 1927 over 1926 is estimated by those who are well qualified to make a computation as being between four and five million pounds. In the four western provinces they have been building up a magnificent dairy industry. In 1910 the production in those provinces was less than 7,000.000 pounds of butter. That production grew in 1920 to 28,000,000 pounds. In 1925 it reached a total of 1,000,000 pounds a week, or 52,000,000 pounds a year. In 1926 it reached a total of 55,000,000 a year, and we are informed by members of the National Dairy Council of Canada, who are well qualified to make an estimate in regard to this matter, that the production in those provinces for the year ending March 31st next will be over 10,000,000 less than it was in the preceding year.
I should like to represent the situation to the minister in another way. We have been
saying a great deal about inducing people to come to this country to fill up our vacant lands and engage in farming. If you hope to succeed in inducing people to go on Canadian farms you must give them encouragement by holding out to them the prospect of profitable employment or reasonable profits. Take the average butter production of the average Canadian cow. I believe it is about 150 pounds a year, but we will put it at 200 pounds if you like. The production of some ten million pounds of butter which we import from New Zealand and Australia in one year would keep fifty thousand cows busy the year round in the Dominion of Canada. If you allow ten cows to a farm, that would establish or play a very important part in establishing a firm basis of mixed farming on some five thousand farms in this Dominion. What are we doing by this arrangement with Australia and New Zealand? By this foolish policy of the government we are establishing on a paying basis mixed farms, not in British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Alberta and other provinces, but in Australia and New Zealand. We are importing from Australia and New Zealand millions of pounds of butter which should and can be produced in -this country, and we are exporting every year, to go into the pockets of the farmers of Australia and New Zealand, millions of dollars which should be in the pockets of our own farmers.
Our exports and imports are very suggestive. In 1925, for instance, we exported
24.500.000	pounds of butter and we imported
193.000	pounds, so that we had a surplus of exports of more than 24,000,000 pounds. Our product was going out to other countries of the world and their money coming into Canada to enrich our farmers. In the fiscal year 1926 our exports amounted to 23,303,900 pounds, and our imports to 7,029,000 pounds. In 1927 our exports dropped from 23,303,900 pounds to 9,878,400 pounds, and our imports amounted to 7,190,267 pounds.. For the year 1928 it looks very much as if we would have
10,000,000 pounds of imports in excess of our exports and. in fact, it looks as if our exports would be practically nothing at all. Therefore, as regards the dairy industry, after two and a half years' experience with this foolish trade arrangement with Australia and New Zealand, we have a net result of our exportable surplus of 24 000,000 pounds being wiped out entirely and being replaced with an importation of more than 10,000,000 pounds of butter.
May I point to another fact? The United States imposes a duty of twelve cents a pound
Supply-Agriculture

on Canadian buttter. Surely every hon. member representing a dairy constituency and looking for future markets, would like to 6ee the United States reduce that tariff against our butter, but do you think there is any likelihood of the United States doing so, as long as Canada permits Australia and New Zealand to send millions of pounds of their butter into this country at a rate of duty of one cent a pound? Will the United States lower their tariff and thus make Canada a halfway house for huge importations of butter from New Zealand and Australia? I do not think so, because the United States have followed a policy of protecting their farmers by giving them an advantage in their home markets over outside competitors. That is the sensible and rational .thing for us to do in this Dominion of Canada.
Another little point which is worth referring to in connection with this matter is this. We all know by the advertisements and posters which we see put up all over Canada that, in the harvest season in the west, men are invited to come from other parts of the country to assist the western farmers in taking off their harvest. One of the advantages in going into mixed farming would be to encourage the farmer in Manitoba, Saskatchewan or Alberta to hire at least one man by the year, to give one man employment the year round, to give him something to do in the winter time as well as in the summer. But under this arrangement with Australia and New Zealand, with the dairy industry [DOT] going out of business, with farmers getting rid of their cows, they have nothing for a man to do in the winter time, the result being that hundreds of men, who were formerly employed in assisting farmers to take care of their stock during the winter, find themselves during the winter months out of employment. That is inevitable.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), in advocating this arrangement, advised us to sell our butter to the old country; he told us to ship our surplus butter, if we had any, to London, and to import butter from Australia and New Zealand. In the first place, if we ship our butter to the old country, it will cost us about five cents per pound to get it from the prairie provinces to England. In the second place, when we get it there we are forced to compete with all the other butter-producing countries of the world that have a surplus. In the third place, if we ship a pound of butter from, say Saskatoon or Regina to London, England, at a cost of five cents a pound, and bring a pound of butter from New Zealand or Australia to Saskatoon 
or Regina, that will cost another five cents per pound, so that by the plan advocated by the Minister of Finance there is a direct loss of ten cents per pound. That strikes me as foolish and illogical in the extreme.
I looked in the returns to see to what extent Australia and New Zealand were providing our farmers with a market and I found that in 1926 our exports of butter to Australia were nil and our exports to New Zealand amounted to ten dollars' worth. I imagine some people in New Zealand were wondering what sort of people we had in Canada who could make such a foolish bargain, and why it was we did not produce our own butter. Evidently they decided to order a pound or so of our butter, in order to find out what kind of butter we produced in Canada, and I am sure they found that butter made in any province in Canada was equal to the best made in any part of the world. We thus got ten dollars of their money. In 1926, we exported to the United States only 17,774 pounds of butter. Why? Because it costs twelve cents per pound to import butter into that country. That is a very good reason. The United States say to us in Canada: We have farmers here who can produce butter, and while it is true you make good butter in Canada, we do not want your butter. We do not intend to allow you to send your butter into this country to be consumed by our people. We intend to give our own farmers an opportunity of supplying our people with butter.

Has the hon. member the
figures in regard to the increase or otherwise in the export of milk or cream or cheese?
I am dealing with butter.

But it is very important
to get them all together.

I	quite
agree it is very important. These are the figures of our imports of butter from Australia and New Zealand in 1925 and 1926:

There is at the present time a demand in the United States, in New York state particularly, for milk and cream from the province of Ontario. I suppose my hon. friend is aware of the fact that in the state of New York-and I presume in other states across the line, but I know it is the case in the state of New York-they have been year after

Supply

Agriculture
year, putting into effect this tuberculin test with their cattle. They are determined to have all their cattle in that state accredited herds, with the result that they have wiped out thousands of cattle in the state of New York, and to a certain extent wiped out their local production, and that I submit furnishes a good reason why there is a demand in New York state to-day, not only for Ontario and Quebec milk and cream, but also for cattle and milch cows from these provinces. That accounts for it to a very large extent.
But I should like the minister, or some member on the other side of the house, particularly someone from Alberta or Saskatchewan. to give this committee some good, tangible and commonsense reason why we should put our dairymen in the western provinces in the position they are in. I have given some figures for the west, but the statement also applies to the east and affects the dairymen of Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes. It affects the price which the farmers of Ontario and Quebec get for their cheese. They are beginning to feel the effect of this Australian and New Zealand arrangement in the price of cheese. That was reflected in the prices paid last season for Ontario and Quebec cheese. It has a wide effect, but will some person tell me, will my hon. friend from Lisgar inform me, why we should allow New Zealand to send millions of pounds of butter into Canada at one cent a pound and Canada get absolutely nothing in return for that? In so far as the arrangement with Australia is concerned, it might be said that we offset what we lose in the dairying industry by the advantages, if there be any, to the pulp and paper manufacturers and to the automobile concerns. But you cannot say that in regard to New Zealand, and we are getting more butter from New Zealand than from Australia. Why then should this arrangement with Australia, which was bad enough in all reason, be extended, as it was, to New Zealand, giving them the advantage of our market and getting nothing whatever in return? Of course under the arrangement we have the privilege of paying more for raisins in Canada. That was intended for the special benefit of the people of Australia and was one of those things which was liberally coated with oil, in order that it could be more easily swallowed by hon. members from the west, and even the free traders from the west took that down without even making a face, swallowed it as nicely and easily as anything you could imagine. It is a fact that the farmers of Australia and New Zealand have a very decided advantage in the climate
which they enjoy as compared with the climate of Canada. It is a fact that you can produce milk from which butter is made on grass cheaper than you can in winter time, when the stock has to be housed and supplied with expensive feed. What about those people in Australia and New Zealand whose cattle range out the year round? They have a decided advantage, and I should like hon. members in this house to consider this well. You may theorize as much as you like about what John Bright and Cobden and some of those fellows said many years ago. You may theorize as much as you like about free trade and protection, but I say that any government in this country should take into consideration the climatic conditions in Canada in arranging the tariff. The government is not fair to the farmers who have to spend thousands of dollars in putting up expensive bams and stables in which to house their stock, who have to spend thousands of dollars in cutting and storing feed for the stock in winter-stock which during the winter months are, as the farmers very often say, eating their heads off: that is to say they are not producing for him a profit. The farmer is waiting until the next summer to make a profit out of his cattle. Surely it is unfair, unreasonable and unjust in the extreme, to tell a farmer in Ontario or in Quebec or in the western provinces, or in any province, with climatic conditions such as we have in Canada, that he must compete on even terms with the farmers of Australia and New Zealand, who have a decided advantage over the farmers in this country in the matter of climate. This arrangement has been tried out for two and a half years \ it has proved an absolute failure, and we have men from all over Canada, not one or two, but men representing all the dairy organizations in the Dominion, in every province, appealing to this government to put an end to this trade arrangement and give the farmers of Canada a fair deal in the matter of finding a market at home for the things that they produce.

I listened with interest
to the hon. member for Frontenac. I expected the Minister of Agriculture would rise in his seat and offer some defence. I think I said last year, and I repeat it again this year, that you cannot run with the hare and hunt with the hounds. That is, if you believe in low tariff or even free trade, you cannot say "I want free trade in those things which I buy and protection in the things which I sell." This very proposition the hon- member for Frontenac has presented to-day was put up to me in my last election. The people of the
Supply-Agriculture

city of Calgary, when I spoke about free trade in butter and the question of the Australian treaty, told me I would not say the same thing in the rural district, where dairying was being carried on, as I did in the city. I wish to give the hon. member for Frontenac some figures in connection with this matter which I received a few days ago. I had twenty-eight cows myself when I was on a homestead in Alberta, and I told the farmers in the dairying district-and I could name the district- "If you cannot meet the competition of your fellow citizens in the British Empire 8,000 miles away, who have to ship their butter that distance, and send it over the equator, you had better learn to do it or go out of business." In the districts where I made that statement I got the largest vote. I said to them, "How can you, with consistency, ask for a protection on your butter and then send me down to parliament to plead for a reduction of the duty on agricultural implements? It cannot be done.'' I cannot sit still and say that I am going to support a tariff on butter and ask for a reduction of the duty on agricultural implements.
Mr. hon. friend quoted some figures for 1925. I was interested in this question of butter, and when I came here I wrote to the department and asked for facts as regards the imports and exports of butter for 1927. When I heard the hon. member for Frontenac dealing with the question of butter I ran upstairs and got a statement I received the other day which show's that in 1927 we exported butter to the amount of 83,351,581, and that we imported $2,500,000 worth, or nearly a million dollars' worth more butter was exported than imported by us. Those facts surely show that the Canadian butter trade is not suffering very much.

What year
was that?

The fiscal year ending
December 31, 1927. My hon. friend took 1925. I presume that 1927 is much more satisfactory to our farmers and to the house at large. We imported two million dollars' worth of butter, and we exported nine million pounds, or over a million dollars' worth more than we imported.	Why did we do it?
Simply because our butter is good and commands better prices abroad than at home, Why should we put an import duty on butter? Why should we ask our fellow-citizens in the towns and cities to pay more for our butter than the price it commands in the open market? We produce our wheat and 
sell it in the open market against the competition of the world, and we also meet the open market for our butter.

Does my
hon. friend not think that when Canada had a surplus of from twenty to twenty-four million pounds of butter, that surplus was a sufficient guarantee to the Canadian people that they would not have to pay more than they should for Canadian butter at home?

It is a sufficient guarantee that if they could get more for it in the export -market they would send it there. And that is what they did. I do not think, Mr. Chairman, that I need go any further into the matter. Our exports of butter show that even with the Australian treaty in effect Canadian butter is able to meet competition in the markets of the world, and asks for no quarter there. Therefore we do not propose to run with the hare and hunt with the hounds.
