Cold storage warehouses, $30,000.

Have there been any
changes in the distribution of these branches since last year?
No, this is to complete old contracts that were entered into prior to last year.
Are any new ones anticipated for this year?

Yes, we have just
entered into a contract with a cold storage organization in New Westminster. If it makes sufficient progress we may require a further amount in the supplementary estimates to take care of it.
That is to cover agricultural products and fish, or just fish alone?
Everything that is perishable.

Item agreed to.
Fruit, including grant of $8,000 to the Canadian Horticultural Council, $290,000.

The principal increase here, Mr. Chairman, is due to an extension of our grading system for export. It will be recalled that last session legislation was passed authorizing the department to introduce a system of compulsory inspection of apples and other fruit intended for export. This involves a considerable outlay. Five dollars is charged by the department for each car inspected, and this money goes back into the treasury.

Supply-Agriculture

Does this new inspection
give our fruit access to the Australian market?

No, it would not
affect that market.

Do they accept our fruit
there?

There is some fruit going there, but it is not subject to inspection. The objection that our Australian friends have against our fruit is the possibility that fire blight may be brought into the *country. We do not think the disease is transmissible through our fruit.

Is that the only country
which refuses Canadian fruit under those conditions?
No, Japan is another. Some countries are more afraid of the transmission of fire blight than are others.

When we were on a similar item about four years ago the minister was kind enough to promise to give me the reason for the spread between the prices paid to the growers of Delicious apples in the Okanagan valley, and the prices charged by the vendors in the city of Ottawa. They now sell first class Delicious apples at 2 for 15 cents, while the grower in the Okanagan valley, I understand, receives about $1.60 or $1.70 per box of about 140. The inquisitiveness that I had four years ago still persists, and if the hon. minister and his very able assistant can give that information to the people of Canada, I am sure it will interest both the consumer here and the grower in the Okanagan valley.

I think the spread is due to high freight and express rates and the high cost of handling. It might have been attributable four years ago to the activities of the combine that was then in operation. This has since been dissolved, so after all perhaps the spread was not so much attributable to that cause as we thought at the time. I remember the interrogation of my hon. friend, but it was made so long ago that I forgot to anticipate it on this occasion. Possibly we can get the information.
I did not expect the minister could give it to me offhand, but it would be most interesting to know how that spread occurs.
Yes.
Has the government or the minister's department in the past made any attempt to minimize this spread?

The fruit branch
thought they were working along proper lines when they assisted the commissioner to gather information in respect to the Nash combine We worked on that for nearly two years. Anyhow the growers are always afraid of combines, whether they be \?heat combines or tobacco combines or any other kind. We felt it was our duty to assist them in ferreting out the information in connection with this matter and we called the growers together in conference here about two and a half years ago to take counsel with one another. They came from the Atlantic and the Pacific and we paid their expenses, incurring a cost of some $1,600. We gave them an opportunity to organize their forces in the direction of a national campaign of salesmanship with a view to reducing the costs to which my hon. friend has referred. The main thing in selling satisfactorily is to have a product of good quality, and I will say this for British Columbia: that there are no other people in the Dominion I know of, so far as this or any other commodity is concerned, who have deliberately exceeded the standard required by law. The growers of British Columbia actually put up a pack a standard above that which the law demands and for that reason they can generally find their way into any market in the world.

The minister has not
answered my question.

What does the
hon. gentleman want?

I have asked the question a good many times before, I have asked it again to-day, and I will continue to ask it. I want to know what the minister or his department has done in order to put into the pockets of the producers a larger share of the proceeds to which they are entitled considering the vast sum paid by the consumers.

I understood the
hon. gentleman to ask, first, what we had done to reduce the enormous spread, and I tried to answer that question. He also inquired as to what we had done to encourage a more acceptable system of marketing. My hon. friend has missed the point, because I dealt with shipping-point inspection especially in the case of exports. Through such inspection and the granting of the government certificate accompanying each consignment we have done something to help the industry, and the British Columbia and Ontario apple growers assure me that, having experienced the beneficial results of this

Supply-Agriculture
system, they would not now think of shipping their product without a certificate of quality.
That is not the question.

The hon. gentleman does not want to hear that. However, that is the way to bring about satisfactory results and I am anxious to impress it upon him. If there is anything else of a specific character which the hon. gentleman desires to know I shall be glad to answer him. I would ask, however, that he put specific questions and not generalities as to what we have done for this, that and the other. We have met the situation and improved the standing of British Columbia apples on the British market, and this result we have achieved by making grading compulsory for everyone. Ninety per cent of the growers grade their apples voluntarily in any case, and this legislation is to compel the other ten per cent, who have been spoiling the market, to follow suit. What further can I do for my hon. friend?

The minister says that
the government has enhanced the market value of the product, but the proceeds that go into the grower's pocket have not been increased. I want to know what his government can do or has done or contemplates doing in order that the producer may get that larger share to which he is entitled in view of the enormous cost to the consumer.

All matters directly pertaining to production are usually conceded to fall within the scope of the provincial government. One cannot draw a very distinct line of demarcation between federal and provincial responsibility, but we have endeavoured to draw at least a rough line between the two, and all matters relating to improved production and reduced production costs are recognized to devolve upon the provincial government, while matters of grading and marketing as well as of standardization are regarded as coming under the jurisdiction of the federal government. Now I have already told my hon. friend what we have done in respect of the duties which I have classified as falling to us. We do not control freight rates. As I say, we have shipping-point inspection but we have nothing to do with freight rates, although we have made representations in this regard. Indeed, I made such representations when I was in the .provincial government, but we have no particular record of any results achieved. The question has been raised on more than one occasion regarding express

and freight rates on apples, but I cannot offhand indicate what has been the outcome of any representations that have been made in the matter. The rates are still very high, however.

Probably I am stupid,
but I want to get an answer to a definite question, and apparently I cannot convey my idea, to the minister, or else he is stealthily evading the point. In the years he has been Minister of Agriculture, what has he done to find out, first, what the spread consists of and, secondly, whether that spread cannot be minimized so that the producer may receive more for his goods? Surely that is a simple question.

Does my hon.
friend suggest that we should start an investigation into the costs of handling at each end? Well, we did do that. The combine was charging a double commission, as my hon. friend will remember, and they were fined several hundred thousand dollars; double commissions were considered to be illegal. The courts confirmed that finding and this evil was removed. I think my hon. friend will admit that this is something.
That is one achievement; what next?

My hon. friend, I
see, remembers that. Does he think we should go before the railway board and ask them to call a hearing? I repeat, we brought the fruit growers from various parts of Canada into conference, the department paying the cost, and they could have taken advantage of that trip to request a hearing before the railway commission if they wanted to make representations regarding freight or express rates. That is as far as we have gone.

The minister has told us what great care is taken in British Columbia in the grading and packing of their apples, and he has said that due to the fact that they exceed the legal standard they have no difficulty in finding a market. That is very good. Now what I understand my hon. friend (Mr. McGibbon) to have in mind is this: We all know, and we can easily satisfy ourselves if we walk down the street, that we are paying a high price for apples in Ottawa, as indeed we pay for them anywhere else in Canada, in the east at any rate. We can also easily ascertain this to be the fact, that the producer of apples in British Columbia, for instance, notwithstanding all the care he takes in the selection, packing

Supply-Agriculture
and grading of his apples, does not get for his product anything like a remunerative price considering the great care and labour he expends, and the capital invested. Perhaps the minister has under his hand the figures in this regard and I should like him to disclose them so as to satisfy my curiosity. He might tell us the extent of the importations of similar fruit from across the line into British Columbia. I have been informed that growers in California and Washington and Oregon, finding a market at home for all their produce, are left with a surplus which they are obliged either to throw out into the back yard to rot, or else to ship into Canada, taking whatever they can get for it. That fruit is sent into the prairie provinces at prices far below its cost of production.
Would that increase the spread?

I am trying to find out if this has not something to do with the low price received by the British Columbia producer for his apples. The American producer says, "Here is a box of apples which cost me about $5 to produce; I might better sell it for $2 than throw it out in the ba.ck yard", and we allow him to ship it in Canada and take the market which should be kept for British Columbia apples- This cheap fruit is dumped into the prairie provinces, with the natural result that the British Columbia producer has to come down in his price. That is the point. I think the minister understands that, and perhaps he has the figures which would indicate to what extent the importation of apples from the United States into the western provinces has been carried on.
The total importation?

Yes, from
the United States into the western provinces.

I have not the
total by provinces, but I have the total importation of apples into Canada for 1927, which amounted to 151,568 barrels. I also have a list of all the other fruits if my hon. friend cares to have it.
Have there been any complaints from Canadian producers in regard to the dumping into Canada of apples or any other fruits at sacrifice prices?

Only 525 barrels of [DOT]apples came into Canada under the dumping clause, because as you know the invoice price has to be below the set price before the dumping clause is applied. That amounts to only 56103-29
0.34 per cent of the total. The rest of the apples came in at a higher invoice price, consequently the dumping clause was not applied.

Is that for
last year?
Yes-

Did I understand the
minister to say that over 150,000 barrels of apples were imported into the three western provinces?
Into all Canada.

I should like to ask the minister whether the application of section 43 of the Customs Act to the importation of fruits into the western provinces from the United States would not. make it impossible for low priced fruit to be dumped there from the United States?

Section 43 was applied to 525 barrels of apples, which was only about one-third of one per cent of the total. These were low grade apples brought in at low prices, and consequently the dumping, clause was applied. The remainder of the apples were of' a superior quality and came in above the set price, and therefore the dumping clause was not applied to them.

I do not know to what extent fruit is being dumped into the prairie provinces from the United States, but I have never seen any of it at these low prices. In the particular district in which I reside the whole problem is to buy the fruit. We realize that our friends in British Columbia produce excellent fruit which we wish to purchase, fruit which we need and which we should have. We live in a cold country and are not able to grow this fruit ourselves, and in the winter time it makes an excellent food to balance up the heavier foods used on the farms. We need apples and other British Columbia fruits, and it seems to me that we have the very best market there for British Columbia fruit if we could afford to buy it. I do not maintain that our friends in British Columbia get too much for their products, because we know that is not the case. I know many men who have left their farms on the prairies to go into the fruit districts of British Columbia in an attempt to make a living growing fruit, and a great many of them have come back to the prairies after having lost money. Certainly there is not very much money in growing fruit in British Columbia, but I think the trouble lies more in faulty distribution than in the tariff or anything else. I can hardly ever buy a box of apples in my village for less than

Supply-Agriculture

$4, and certainly not for less than $3. The average farmer on the prairies should be able to put in from 20 to 40 boxes of apples every year for the use of his family, but not one farmer out of ten can afford to do it. I believe there is a great field for investigation there; perhaps this work could be done cooperatively. If fruit is dumped into the prairie provinces from the United States it certainly does not reach our part of the country. I do not believe the retailers make too much of a profit either, but the problem seems to b.e in distribution. The fruit is shipped in carload lots to the larger centres and shipped out again over long distances, sometimes as far as 300 miles or more, in less than carload .lots, which means extra freight and express, all of which makes the price to the consumer almost prohibitive. I would suggest to our friends in British Columbia that they explore this field and see if it is not possible to develop some marketing system in the nature of our wheat pool, which would enable them to distribute these apples themselves to the smaller centres. They could ship the fruit in carloads, which would give us the benefit of the cheaper freight, and if that could be done and the fruit sold at a reasonable price there is hardly any limit to what we could consume on . the prairies. I was going to say our fruit consumption could be doubled, but I can easily say that it could be increased five or ten times. We have the capacity for the consumption of that much more fruit, but the prices are so high that we are unable to buy the quantity we could use.

I am glad to secure some information from a private member which I could not get from the government. The remarks of the hon, member (Mr. Campbell) at least have a ring of sincerity and common sense. This is one of the problems before Canada to-day, and I think the minister and his department should devote some attention to the question of distribution. If something could be done along this line he would be performing a service to the producer and the consumer which would be far greater than anything he has done in the past. I hope the minister will take into consideration the suggestions of the last speaker, and also see if he cannot give us a little more information with regard to that branch of the industry.

If it will help my friend at all I will take a moment or two to recite some of the things we hope to do in the next twelve months. Last year, in reply to an inquiry by one of the hon. members for St. John as to what we contemplated doing

in aid of cooperative marketing, I pointed out that I hoped not to have to organize any new branches of my department until I had better office accommodation for them, but that as soon as I secured that accommodation it was my hope to organize a cooperative marketing branch. My department was then scattered around in eighteen or twenty buildings throughout this city, and I did not want to increase that number to twenty-one. However, events have travelled pretty fast since then. There is, for example, the situation in Essex and Kent in regard to the cooperative marketing of tobacco. The efforts of the growers in that respect have met with only partial success. My deputy and myself went up to study the situation at Chatham, and later on at Windsor, and we made an announcement as to what would be done. We had not accommodation for our present staff, but the situation was growing so serious in Essex and Kent that we felt the time had come to establish a cooperative marketing branch and to take our chances of finding accommodation for it when it was established. The report to council asking for the necessary authority has been signed, and it will go to the treasury board in a day or two. There will be a staff of five.
That, probably, is the information my hon. friend desired. The branch is not yet in operation, and I do not know how long a period will elapse before it will be. We find that to get anything through the civil service commission it takes at least ninety days, so I give fair warning if any delay is experienced in the matter.

This is truly a wonderful government. They have been in office since 1922, and in 1928 the Minister of Agriculture comes down solemnly and tells the house that the reason he has not done anything in this matter is because he has not got an office.
I ask you, Mr. Chairman, was ever a more absurd excuse offered to an intelligent body of men? He has not got an office! After six or seven or eight years in that department that is the excuse offered by the minister for not having done anything for the people of this country.
Oh, listen!

I was going to ask the minister if he has distributed any information regarding the keeping of fruit. Of course it is well known you can keep fruit, notably apples, in certain temperatures, and they are kept that way by every large wholesaler; but when apples reach the small stores and the

Supply-Agriculture
consumer many bags are possibly spoiled by the exposure of the fruit to a fairly high temperature such as you would find in a kitchen. Then the apple becomes unattractive and people do not consume as many as they otherwise would. The idea has often suggested itself to me that if the government distributed a bulletin on how to keep fruit it would have a most beneficial result and no doubt bring about a larger consumption.
Yesterday7 we had a very interesting debate on research work. We are consuming in this country large quantities of the juices of citrus fruits for breakfast, and I was going to suggest to the minister that he might take up with the research council the question of finding out whether it is not possible to secure some very palatable substitute for these citrus fruits for breakfast, and by doing so increase the market for fruits produced in this country.

We sent a number of packages of fruit, both last year and this year, to Great Britain. These were packed in different ways-some with two tiers, and some with one-just to find out how much the fruit was affected in transit by the depth of the package. We also had some experiments conducted in the last two or three years in regard to the breaking down of the Jonathan apple, and these have shown that a great deal of improvement could be obtained by harvesting at the right time. I think a great deal more can be done. Too great care cannot be exercised in handling not only apples but other commodities for export. The least thumb mark or the least roughness in handling will be shown immediately the commodity arrives on the other side of the water. I remember some of our people were visitng at Harrod's and they found in the case of some Canadian apples fhat although they had been handled with the greatest possible care thumb marks were visible on the skin. It is not possible, I repeat, to take too much care in order to ensure the arrival of fruit at its destination in good condition.

In regard to the matter of keeping fruit I was very much impressed in London in 1921 when I was handed some apples that were over a year and a half old. They had just been taken out of storage where they had been kept at the right temperature. The apples were Ontario spies and they were in first class condition.

I should like to ask if the vote of $8,000 to the Canadian Horticultural Council is to be continued. It has been passed for a number of years, and no one 56103-294
objects to voting this money when it is to be used for the advancement of horticulture. But when that vote, or any portion of it, is used in support of an appeal to the tariff board for higher protection on the fruit that the people of this country need to consume I think it is time to enter a protest. I certainly do protest against voting any money to the Canadian Horticultural Council, or any other organization, to enable them to appear before the tariff board and ask for a higher tariff.

I presume they want to look after only what they conceive to be the interests of the fruit industry. On the other hand there is the Consumers' League, a very active body under the direction of a very prominent gentleman, looking after activities such as those of the horticultural council.

But there is no vote
for them.

I think there are
a few items with respect to them all right.

I should like to ask
the minister in what way he finds his action in regard to any office he proposes to establish hampered by the civil service commission? I have heard the minister repeat so often in the house that he is hampered by the civil service commission that I should like to know in what particular way he does find his work hindered.
Mr, MOTHERWELL:	I should have said
the civil service commission under the limitations of the Civil Service Act. I have no complaint at all to make of delay due to the commission, but the procedure laid down is so tortuous that it takes ninety days on an average to get a matter through at all. I noticed in a speech delivered by a member of the previous administration in 1921 that exactly the same condition prevailed at that time. According to a return that was brought down the putting through of a certain matter took ninety days. This is due to no fault of the commission; they act as expeditiously as possible-but to the routine which has to be followed. The first thing we have to do is to establish the position; a position has to be created before you can appoint anyone to it. Then an elaborate description has to be given of the position. Then the matter has to go before the treasury board, who look it over carefully in order to be sure that I am not exceeding my powers. They have kept a very watchful eye on these matters for the last two or three years. There is a
Supply-Agriculture

lot of routine, and each party through whose hands the matter goes has to perform his duty and see that the necessary requirements are complied with. This all takes time. When I held office elsewhere the procedure was more simple and direct, and when a position was created it did not take nearly so long to fill it. If we required a man we went after him and got him. I have no authority of that nature in my present position. If immediate action is required the minister in charge must have power to act immediately; he cannot secure prompt action in the face of so much routine. The same thing is true with regard to research work. Australia can come to Canada and in broad daylight, take away our best men. Why? Because their research workers are not under the civil service commission of that country. But on the other hand we cannot go to Australia and say to some of their men: "We want you," for the simple reason that we have no such authority.

All the minister has
said will increase my respect and admiration for the civil service commission and convince me all the more that we really need to maintain such an institution in Canada. In spite of what the minister says, I find at every session of parliament some action is taken by this house to impair the usefulness and power of the civil service commission. In the estimates year after year appear votes providing for the appointment of certain officials not under the commission. There seems to be no difficulty whatever on the part of the government to get around the civil service commission when they want to do so, but the minister and one or two of his colleagues use every opportunity they can to throw some mud, not particularly at the personnel of the civil service commission, but at the principle on which the commission is based. In other words, they want the patronage system back. The minister told us about how nicely things were done where he came from, and I presume he refers to Saskatchewan. I can cite some instances about how nicely things are done there too. Let me give one.
In the Department of Agriculture when I was in charge of it?

No. I think the minister administered his department excellently in Saskatchewan, and I will pay him the tribute, as I have done in my constituency, of saying that he is an excellent Minister of Agriculture. Without abusing the old proverb, "comparisons are odious," I think I can say

that the minister understands his particular job just as well as any minister of the crown in this house. I do not think he is any particular sinner with respect to the patronage system. Some time ago I was unfortunate enough to become involved in a law suit in Saskatchewan.

moment, but I think it is particularly relevant. The minister was permitted to express his opinion with regard to the patronage system, a system which is involved in every single vote in this house. I was going to say that in the particular case referred to I found that the provincial police of Saskatchewan were instrumental in working up a civil case against me.

maintopic: ELECTRICITY AND FLUID EXPORTATION ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext: Mr. H. A. STEWART (Leeds) moved the second reading of Bill No. 2, to regulate the exportation of electric power.

maintopic: ELECTRICITY AND FLUID EXPORTATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: ELECTRICITY AND FLUID EXPORTATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I cannot add much to the information which was given to the house on the first reading. The object of the bill is to amend the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act of 1907. By the provisions of that act the exportation of petroleum, natural gas, water and other fluids is regulated by order in council, and the effect of the bill now before the house is to change the provision with respect to the exportation of electric power so as to make it subject to act of parliament, and to leave the regulation of the export of petroleum, natural gas, water and fluids as it now stands-

Electricity and Fluid Exportation
When this legislation was introduced in 1907 the value of electric power was comparatively small as compared with its value at the present time. It is now one of our most valuable resources, and is practically inexhaustible, because as long as water flows over a waterfall we are able to develop electric power. It is constantly increasing in value, and we believe is approaching a huge development in Canada. Its value to Canada can scarcely be over-estimated, and I submit that in dealing with an asset so valuable we should have the sanction and approval of t'he House of Commons rather than have the matter dealt with by order in council. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that the exportation of electric power should, as far as possible, be prohibited; that electric power should be retained in Canada for the benefit of the Canadian' people, because its value in developing our industry and our agriculture and in providing traffic for our railways can hardly be accurately estimated. This bill does not propose to go the length of prohibiting the export of power, but would make it subject to the regulation of parliament. As far as I have observed I think the press comment has been favourable, and the bill as introduced has the support of a very large body of public opinion in Canada. There are provisions in the bill which preserve the rights of the provinces, and the measure contains certain saving clauses with respect to existing liens.
The only objection I have heard urged against the bill in the house or elsewhere is that it does not provide for emergencies, or for the fact that in some cases it may be extremely advantageous that there should be an exchange of power from time to time as we have it at Niagara and perhaps elsewhere. That objection may be easily overcome by a proper amendment. In fact I have gone so far as to draft an amendment which I think would meet all the abjections which have been offered. An order of the house has been made for the production of copies of all licenses and regulations, and when these documents are brought down we shall be able more intelligently to discuss the matter. I suggest that the bill might well be read a second time and sent to committee for approval and consideration and for such amendments as the circumstances seem to warrant.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ELECTRICITY AND FLUID EXPORTATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government
is taking no exception to this bill. It does not make any drastic change, but I think the sponsor has in mind that in cases where new developments spring up, and there is a possibility of a certain portion of the power
being exported, the company or individual promoting the measure shall come to parliament and obtain a private bill for that purpose. With that suggestion, the government has no quarrel; indeed I think I may say on behalf of the government that we will go even a step further. It is in our opinion desirable that the exportation of electricity be absolutely prohibited; it is too valuable an asset for us to permit it to leave our country. Although we may be at some disadvantage from a climatic point of view we have this very valuable asset which to some extent offsets that condition, and it is important that we should retain it within the boundaries of our own country. I suggest that this bill be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines in order to give interested parties an opportunity to appear and voice any objections they may have to its provisions, and also to give my hon. friend an opportunity to make the necessary amendments which I think are required, particularly to clause 6. That clause reads as follows:
Nothing herein contained shall be deemed to affect the rights of any province with respect to power or the rights of any person under any license issued before the first day of January, 1928.
I understand it is the intention of my hon. friend not to interfere with existing contracts, and that the issue of yearly license will continue. With that suggestion I think the bill might go to committee for consideration, and the government will be content,

maintopic: ELECTRICITY AND FLUID EXPORTATION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I
should like to get some further information on this question. My hon. friend has made a statement about not interfering with provincial rights. Last year we had a discussion in Alberta with regard to these power rights, and I understand the provinces of Ontario and Quebec claimed that they had full rights to the development of electrical energy in their respective provinces. It seems to me that if the provinces control the generation and distribution of electricity, this bill may be an interference with provincial rights. If we are to continue to put an embargo on the exportation of electric power, there is no reason why a similar embargo should not be imposed on the exportation of gas and other natural resources under provincial control. I think it should be made clear how far we are going to trespass on provincial rights.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the select standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
Post Office Act

Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Toronto Northwest) moved the second reading of Bill No. 22. to amend the Post Office Act.
He said:	The object of this bill Mr. Speaker, is well known to the press of Canada, namely, to identify the ownership of newspapers. For many years past the newspapers of this country have been coming to parliament and securing privileges. Up to 1882 newspapers were carried free by the post office. This bill provides for what is already required by law in England, Australia and the United States, that is: A sworn statement of the names and addresses of editors, owners and principal stockholders of every newspaper, magazine, periodical or other publication, to be fded with the Postmaster General semiannually. There is an exception in favour of religious, fraternal, temperance and scientific or other similar publications. Also, it shall not be necessary to include in such statement the names of small stockholders, that is, persons owning less than one per cent of the total amount of the stock, bonds, mortgages or other securities. If any such publication fails to comply with these provisions it shall be' denied .admission to the mails. Paid editorials and other reading matter for which money is paid shall be plainly marked " advertisement ". Statements under the act are to be made in duplicate and delivered to the' Postmaster General, who shall make regulations for the carrying out of the provisions of the act.
I introduce this legislation solely in the interests of the freedom of the press in a liberty-loving country. It is the law to-day, as I have said, in the old land, in Australia and in the United States. Unless a newspaper is registered in the names of the editor, the publisher and the largest stockholders it cannot get the advantage of the mails in the United States, and if it contains paid editorials they must be marked as advertisements.
It is interesting to recall, Mr. Speaker, that you were the pioneer in this field, because away back in 1919 you introduced a resolution for a purpose similar to that which I am now seeking to accomplish by this bill. It was then felt that such legislation was necessary, and parliament was prepared to enact it, but unfortunately at that time we had the so-called uplift form of government known as the Union government, which was very fond of making a political football of any economic question. The then president
[Mr. Adshend.)
of the1 council, Mr. Rowell, raised the point that under section 92 of the British North America Act your proposal affected property and civil rights, and these being under provincial jurisdiction he asked that your motion might stand. His opinion prevailed.

The reading public are entitled to information regarding the ownership of the publications they read. The St. Catharines Standard says:
The information will be very interesting when it comes to the demand for power concessions and other rights, and might explain some flip-flops in the days immediately preceding an election.

Post Office Act
The Globe, founded by George Brown, has urged such legislation for years, and in a recent editorial it says:
Parliament should earnestly support and pass the bill once more introduced by Mr. T. L. Church, requiring newspapers to give to the public information as to their ownership. It is a step which newspapers themselves should welcome in the interest of honest journalism.
Newspapers are a recognized force in the making of public opinion, which means a force in the government of the country. They present the news, but they also present opinions. Readers should know what interests and influences are at work in the forming of the opinions presented. There should be means of judging whether these opinions are based on informed zeal for public welfare or whether the newspaper uttering them is secretly promoting selfish purposes.
It should not be possible for two newspapers under the same ownership to promote contradictory policies without the public knowing the fact. By adopting the wise measure introduced by Mr. Church, the newspapers will be better served and public confidence will be increased.
The Port Hope Guide has this to say in support of the bill:'
The public has a right to know from what source the fountain of public opinion, represented by the press, draws its inspiration. If from interests adverse to the welfare of the public, the fact should be known from the house-tops. This country cannot afford to have the press muzzled or controlled by corporations, parties or persons whose only object is to direct public opinion into lines that are calculated to advance private or corporate interests to the detriment of the general interests of Canadians. _ No responsible publisher, or newspaper owner is ashamed or afraid to allow the whole world to know who's who, and would welcome such a law: it is only the publishing company whose personnel is represented by "straw men" and against such companies action cannot be taken owing to the fog surrounding them. It must not be lost sight of either that there are corporations even in Canada, which can and do afford not only newspapers but radio broadcasting to disseminate what they would have the public believe. Even the electorate might be influenced to vote for some fraudulent scheme and promote a wrong.
I may observe, Mr. Speaker, that you yourself supported a similar resolution in 1919. For your views on the subject I would refer the house to the debate as reported in Hansard. I want it understood that I am not for a moment attacking the press of this country; I do not believe that you could find anywhere a press to excel it. The contribution which the Canadian newspapers made to the community, the country, education, to social betterment, the satisfactory outcome of the war; what it did to promote the cause of the poor and needy and of charity and philanthropy and to further every worthy movement in behalf of the soldiers and of the nation at large, was invaluable. It was the press that helped very
largely to restore Canada to her normal position. Nor can one say too much for the honour and integrity of the press of Canada. The tendency of our Canadian newspapers is decidedly forward, not backward, and notwitstanding the high cost of material and labour their prospects are bright. I have no doubt that the genius of our newspapers will help to make this country great industrially so that Canada will march triumphantly on from strength to strength. The genius of a free people will help and work for the good and success of the newspaper industry.
The object of this bill is to make the disclosure of newspaper ownership compulsory. There are four estates in the Dominion: the Governor General, the Senate, the House of Commons and the press. We know who the Governor General is, we know who the members of the Senate and the House of Commons are, and logically we ought to know the composition of the fourth estate, the press. There is no reason why the ownership of newspapers in this country should not be disclosed, when we bear in mind the fact that registration is compulsory in all cases of transfer of real and personal estate and, as well, in transactions in connection with chattel mortgages, bills of sale, wills, deeds, mortgages, notes, liens and so forth. The shareholders and directors of banks must also be disclosed, and those comprising bank mergers are not concealed. Why, therefore, should the ownership of a newspaper be concealed? A free press is as necessary to the welfare of the country as a free parliament. You, Mr. Speaker, are a literary man and a lawyer, and you presented the argument in this case a few years ago, in 1919, in such a manner as must have commended itself to all thinking people. Had your advice been followed in 1919 it would have been a good thing for this country and for the press and a free press and for the liberty of the press.
Is there any fair-minded man in this country who is opposed to this proposition if he has at heart the interests not only of the country but of the very press itself? Legislation similar to this has been found necessary and has proved beneficial in the United States and in England and Australia, and the same reasons that apply there are equally applicable in Canada. The object of the proposed amendment is to facilitate the enforcing of the regulations governing the use of the mails. In a return brought down by the minister it was shown that the country has been suffering a loss of eight millions a year in the payment of cash sub-

sidies to the newspapers in the way of rates granted on the 'carriage iof newspapers through the mails less than the cost thereof to the post office; in other words an eight million dollar subsidy is given them.
Now the government occasionally spends considerable sums of money in advertising and I do not blame them for so doing. It is the duty of the government to keep the public informed on various questions affecting the interests of the people. All governments do this, and it is only natural for them to patronize the papers that support them. I am not complaining of this because I hope I am enough of a sport to realize that it is what others would do. The merchant on Sparks street also is obliged to advertise in the press and if he sells his stock or store must register the same. The merchant cannot sell his goods without registering, nor can the farmer dispose of his stock or crops or produce without complying with the same requirement of a bill of sale. I see no reason therefore why we should not expect the press to do the same and disclose their ownership.
Canada to-day is the happy hunting ground for American millionaires and promoters who are seizing our forests, our timber reserves, our mines, our pulp wood, our water powers, and in the process enlisting the aid of a section of the press. The future of new Ontario is endangered by a small section of the press which boosts the business interests of American millionaires, and we can very well understand why this legislation is being opposed by a few. It is a fact that many of the newspapers carry paid editorials whose sole object is to boost certain policies. The Toronto News, at one time under the direction of Sir John Willison, went so far as to describe Sir James Whitney and Sir Adam Beck and their hydro program as two amateur anarchists, and other newspapers have been known to oppose enterprises which have been undertaken for the good of the common people of the country. I know that a section of the press in the city I come from tried to foist an expenditure of $32,000,000 on the taxpayers in 1914, in connection with the sale of the Toronto Railway Company and Toronto Electric Light'Company to the city. The arbitration gave them in 1922 $12,000,000 for the railway instead of $32,000,000, and that was twice as much as they should have got. The American interests in. this country are by no means lax in asserting themselves, and they do not hesitate to engage the assistance of a section of the press.
The last time-1919-a, resolution of this nature was proposed we had opposition from

the apostles of uplift, the Union government, especially that brand of uplift that finally landed the good old Conservative party in the cemetery. Legislation of the nature now proposed has been found to work admirably in the United States, and the same is true of England and Prance. It is a social necessity, it is an economic necessity, the object of which is to safeguard the interests of the country. I am sorry that neither the government nor some member of the Progressive party saw fit to introduce this bill, especially in view of the fact that the proposal has been openly espoused by agrarian newspapers in the western provinces as well as by many other leading journals in the prairies, of all shades of politics. I cannot understand why it should have been left to a member of the opposition to bring forward a measure of this kind.
One cannot help regretting the tendency of the press to-day to adopt the chain principle; we have chains of'newspapers throughout the country. These chain newspapers have lost their individuality and their potency, and the local colouring and tireless aid which formerly they gave to the municipalities for good government and for legislation for the masses. I may say in this connection that I have a letter from the Postmaster General of the United States in which he says legislation of this kind is working out very satisfactorily in that country, and I believe there is no reason why it should not work here also. I believe this bill should go to the private bills committee, because it involves a very important public principle, and in that committee deputations could be heard dealing with all sides of the question. I have introduced three' other bills similar to this, but they never proceeded beyond the first reading. Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Toronto Northwest) moved the second reading of Bill No. 26, to amend the Railway Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Explain.

The object of this bill is
a step forward for a national coal policy and to provide a remedy for the existing problem of supplying coal to the central and other portions of Canada, and render Canada independent of foreign supply.
The present coal situation is grave and demands an immediate solution and the adoption of a national fuel policy so that every pound of coal shall be mined and coked under the British flag.
The bill is an effort to establish a national policy for the carriage of Canadian coal and coke on the same basis as is provided by the special tariff on grain and flour. The govern-
Railway Act

ment by an order in council rescinded and then restored special rates on grain and flour. The coal question is a transportation question to the extent of 95 per cent. Canada owns the national railways and merchant marine, and has the facilities to solve the coal problem and put in force a national coal policy which would forever make the country independent of a foreign supply. Action is wanted. Coal is as much a necessity as flour and grain. Part of the Canadian grain going through American channels gets a special rate. There should be equality of treatment for carrying coal on the same basis as flour and grain. Canada has spent over two billions of dollars on the national railways, and surely it ought to be possible to reduce the rates for the carriage of coal by a few cents a ton in order to aid the miner in Alberta and the maritimes. The national railway either belongs to the people of Canada, or it belongs to Sir Henry Thornton. Should it be used to develop a sparsely populated vast dominion, or should it be run solely for profit to satisfy the ambition of its president? Is present profit its sole aim, or is to develop a vast dominion its sole object? Was this railway system taken over by the nation to help bring about economic annexation to the United States, or was the initial objective a means for the distribution of necessities and the transportation of its settlers in order to encourage an ever increasing and contented people? Can a country known to possess a real winter or fully one-half of every year expect to grow if the statement once was noised abroad that no reliable source of fuel was ensured for its settlers? If a country does not grow, will or can its revenue increase? Would not this bill bring in the near future great development of industry, some ten, some twenty and some a hundred' fold?
The legislatures of Alberta and Ontario, and others as well, have lined up in favour of this legislation. There is only one proper course to follow and that is to grant reduced rates for the transportation of coal mined and coked in Canada and used for domestic purposes in Canada in order that the needs of the people may be met in a satisfactory and adequate manner. This particular legislation will cost the country little or nothing, and will confer a great benefit not only on the people of Alberta, and of ether parts of the west, but also on the people of the maritime provinces and of central Canada. It is a step in the right direction.
The management of the national railways say they cannot carry coal from Alberta at 
less than $9 a ton. I would say to Sir Henry Thornton that Canada's national railway system must not be operated for the promotion of the United States coal barons alone but for the benefit of the people of Canada. Sir Henry Thornton receives his salary from the people of Canada. Does he consider their interest one iota or is he striving for his own vain glory? This question has been before the public for six or seven years now, and no progress has been made with it-a football has been made of it.
There is only one way of solving this question and that is along the lines of the Duncan report which is the principle of this bill. Ontario and Quebec are just as much entitled to relief in the coal situation as other portions of the country which receive bonuses and subsidies to solve their economic ills.
The province of Alberta is certainly entitled to a reduced rate for the carriage of coal as are the maritimes and on the same rate cut as grain and flour now receive. There should be equality of treatment in Canada. There Should be an economic policy adopted in this country for the good of all the provinces. It should be a cooperation with a policy of "each for all and all for each." That is the just principle for all provinces in the confederation.
The. proposed legislation may be looked upon as a small form of subsidy, but it will reap a vast harvest, not only for the national railways but for the people of western and central Canada and the east as well. If Sir Henry Thornton is working for the United States coal barons, and himself, he should either be paid solely by them or he should forfeit his present salary to his ambition for a surplus profit. Seemingly Sir Henry Thornton would prefer to fix the coal rate at $9 or $10 a ton and carry no Canadian coal at all, than to lower the charge a trifle and secure the cream of the business. In my opinion a case has been made out for placing coal on a parity with grain and flour in the matter of railway rates on a special tariff toll basis. If hon. members will read the evidence given before the railway commission they will realize that such is the fact and that coal should receive the same preferential rates. For the reasons I have given I move the second reading of the bill.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals): Mr. Speaker, it is my duty to endeavour to inform the house as to what the effect would be upon the rates with which this bill seeks to deal. In the first place the present Crowsnest pass rates

Railway Act
on grain are applicable to the head of the lakes. As regards the movement of coal from the west to Toronto, the rate for grain per ton and the rate for coal per ton are now identical. The rate on grain from the west to Toronto is $12.70 per ton. From Drum-heller, the mining centre to Toronto, the rate is the same. I presume however that my hon. friend who introduced the bill has in mind the application of the same mileage rates as now apply to grain as far as Fort William, to the remainder of the distance from Fort William to Toronto, although the language of the bill which he introduces leaves me somewhat in doubt as to whether that would be the result. Neveretheless I thought it desirable to have figures taken out which would illustrate the application of the mileage scale of the Crowsnest grain rates to Fort William, also to the remainder of the distance to Toronto on coal. The reason for making this analysis was to ascertain whether or not the adoption of such a principle would make it possible to move coal from Drum-heller to Toronto and sell it there to the satisfaction of the people of that city and the people of Ontario generally.
If I remember correctly the representations which have been made by the coal operators of Alberta and by the government of that province, they do not believe that a tate of more than seven dollars per ton would enable the business to be done. All the argument is in the direction of a rate of seven dollars per ton or less in order to make practicable the movement of coal from Alberta to Toronto and southern Ontario generally. If we apply my hon. friend's measure in the manner I have just indicated, the Crowsnest mileage scale east of Fort William as well as west thereof, to coal, we would get a rate from Drumheller to Toronto of $8.44 per ton. That is what the railway commission would be ordered under this legislation to put into effect as a rate, and I submit for the consideration of my hon. friend and those who I know are interested in securing a solution to this question, that a rate of $8.44 is not in accordance with the claims which are made by the coal operators in Alberta and the consuming public in Ontario as to the reduction necessary in order to bring about effective relief.
Is that all rail to Toronto?

Yes. The all-rail rates are the only rates affected by the bill. It might be claimed that a more advantageous comparison from the point of view of coal movement could be secured by including together the statutory rate on grain to Fort William and the rate fixed by the railway commission over the Transcontinental line to Quebec on grain and applying the mileage scale on grain east of Armstrong to the distance to Toronto. I have had those figures taken out too, and the result if that were applied-and I doubt very much if such an application would be covered by the terms of my hon. friend's bill-would be that the rate would still be $8.30 per ton. Therefore we see that by applying the lowest scale rate existent anywhere in Canada with reference to grain, we would still have a rate from the coal fields to the consumer in Ontario of $8.30 a ton. I think I cannot do better than leave to the house the question whether it is desirable to incorporate in the Railway Act a statutory rate which admittedly will not accomplish the objective which the promoter of the bill states that he has in view, because the rate which would be secured thereby is much higher than that stated by the coal operators and the government of Alberta and by the government and people of Ontario as being necessary in such a case. I would be quite prepared on behalf of the government to have the figures I have presented further examined by a committee of the house-and I am not now discussing, as I did the other day, the desirability of further extending the principle of statutory rates-but I think any examination would reveal the accuracy of what I have stated with respect to the application of the measure.
Perhaps it would be worth while to give some information regarding comparative rates from the maritime provinces region on coal with the Crowsnest rate now existing in the west on grain. I know there is a good deal of misunderstanding in some quarters in that connection. The rate on coal to Riviere du Loup, 718 miles, is $2.90 per. ton. The grain rate under the Crowsnest pass schedule for the same distance in western Canada is $3.80 per ton.
Different classifications.

Of course coal and grain are different classifications, but the bill seeks to place them in the same classification. If my hon. friend's bill were to pass, I take it that the rate on coal from the maritime provinces to Riviere du Loop would be increased from $2.90 to $3.80 per ton, and would thus deprive the maritime provinces of the advantages which are theirs at present under the Maritime Freight Rates Act.

Seed, feed and fertilizer control, including grants to seed fairs, etc., §375,000.

Is the
minister extending the operations of the seed control branch to western Canada?

Perhaps I could
answer that question better by pointing out that in all Canada there are six seed control zones, beginning at the western part of Canada. The first one is at Calgary, then Winnipeg, then Toronto, Quebec, Sackville, and there is a central zone in Ottawa. These are used primarily for the testing of seeds for purity from weed seeds and germination. There is a good deal of agitation in the west in regard to paying more attention to the cleaning and preparing of seed. The appliances there are so primitive that it costs so much that the average man cannot pay the cost of properly cleaned seeds. I have been in communication with the Minister of Agriculture of Alberta and the Minister of Agriculture of Saskatchewan in connection with doing co-operative work in connection with these facilities for seed cleaning purposes with the seed men. This vote covers seed, feed and fertilizer. I remember when we came down here the first year the hon. member for Lisgar brought to my attention the very urgent necessity of some amendment to the Feed Act, particularly with reference to bran and shorts. At that time a large percentage of the screenings was included in the bran and shorts. It helped out considerably from the weed standpoint, but not in the feeding properties. We had that act before us several times, and I think now everybody is satisfied with the Feed Control Act in that respect. The particular kind of fertilizers is not of very much interest to the western farmers. We have had experiments with the use of the fertilizers out there and it costs more to distribute it, even if it were laid down on the farm free, than it is worth. But down in eastern Canada where the early virginity is out of the land, the artificial fertilizer becomes an important matter indeed, particularly where you are constantly growing crops like potatoes and tobacco. It is a very vital matter to the farmers to get a good supply of the proper quality. It is just as important to them as any other subject is important to the western farmer-the grading of the grain, for instance.
These three acts, plus the Insecticides Act, which was passed last year, all come under the seed control administration. The Insecticides Act covers all poisons for economic purposes-fruity vegetables or anything else. That is roughly what the seed control commissioner has to do.

The
point I wish to stress is with respect to the control of seed that is being used generally over the western provinces. We have made progress by the establishment of tuberculosis-free areas, pure-bred sire areas, and so on, and I think there is a great field of usefulness for seed control work in western Canada. We have a large number of varieties of grain sold in the same district, and when the crop is drawn to market we get mixed grades.

My hon. friend is speaking of commercial seed. I suppose he saw the survey made by the Dominion Department of Agriculture with regard to the kind of seed used by many farmers. The seed was taken from the drills, and it was found that a large percentage was very low grade and dirty. It was appalling to find this class of seed being sold in what is possibly the premier grain-growing province of the Dominion. We found some of the weed inspectors were doing this, and they above all others should know better. It was not that way twenty years ago; then the utmost care was taken with the seed and it was treated with some form of insecticide. Unfortunately when there is a run of good crops there is a tendency, so far as the bulk is concerned, for the retailer to grow careless with regard to the quality of the seed, with the idea that anything will do.

There is a matter which
should be taken into consideration in connection with this vote, Mr. Chairman. I am sorry that the member for Neepawa (Mr. Milne) is not here, because he and his brother had an unfortunate experience that I think ought not to be repeated very often. The story told to me, if I remember aright, is that they bought some four or five hundred bushels of seed grain on sample from a seed merchant. [DOT] When they got it home they found it was by no means equal to the sample. They complained, but their only satisfaction was to be told that they could draw the grain back to the railway station, about twelve miles away. To draw four or five hundred bushels of seed wheat such a distance at that time of the year was not a welcome experience. The situation must be met by a more rigid control over the men putting seed on the market to see that it is according to sample.
I notice the minister has an increase of $39,000. How is it accounted for?

As my hon. friend will notice, the activities under the department are extending all the time. It costs

something to take care of this insecticide act and also the new hay act. The flat increase that was given to practically all the civil service last year also represents a considerable addition to the vote. There are no particular new activities outside of those mentioned.
