for several years, and the prevailing westerly winds carry the seed out toward the Lethbridge northern irrigation district, on which the province has guaranteed bonds to the extent of over five million dollars. The people in the district have a large enough problem on their hands to make a financial success of the venture without having to contend with perennial sow thistle from Dominion government land. One hon. member near me suggests that we might call it federal sow thistle. I think the minister will agree with me that it is probably one of the worst weeds we have to contend with. Certainly it is a shame that the Dominion government will not provide means to take care of these noxious weeds on their own land. We can deal with farmers in the district by plowing down their crop if they allow noxious weeds to grow unchecked, but we cannot apply this drastic treatment to the Dominion government. Undoubtedly the Dominion authorities might very well spend a little money to take care of their own noxious weeds before offering advice to farmers on the subject. We have absolutely no way of protecting ourselves against noxious weeds growing unchecked on Dominion government lands, and I do hope that the' minister will take the necessary steps this session so that before next session this evil may be checked.

I do not want to
hide behind the Department of the Interior, but really my department has no public lands; these are under the control of the Department of the Interior, and that is where my hon. friend should apply. If there is any way of dealing with this matter through that department I shall be glad to help him. Take the bird sanctuary at Quill lake, which I understand has recently been let for pasturing. As everyone knows, it is swampy. I visited the place a year ago, and I found that sow thistle is getting a hold in the moist ground, in fact it flourishes under such conditions, and without employing an army of men to dig it out by hand I do not know how you can deal with it. There were crops growing on the surrounding land. The lake was swarming with duck, and all the stooks in the vicinity were half eaten up. If I remember rightly, I recommended to my colleague that something be done looking to the closing of that sanctuary. As I say, it has recently been let for pasturing purposes, but that will not solve the eradication of the sow thistle there. My hon. friend I understand is a practical farmer, so he knows that this weed has an under-

Supply-Agriculture
ground root stalk and just revels in moist land. What are you going to do about it? If my hon. friend will give me a recipe for the eradication of that sow thistle I will pass it on to my colleague.

It seems from the minister's
statement that I should be discussing this matter with the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), but I take it that the Minister of Agriculture is the agricultural adviser of his colleague.

I am ready to sit
at my hon. friend's feet and learn on that question.

I am sure now that I have
his sympathy, and that I shall have at least his moral support in endeavouring to get the Minister of the Interior to take care of this problem. The local provincial weed supervisor-I do not know whether that is his correct title-has made several examinations of the patch that I am speaking of, and from what he told me I think he is willing to undertake the necessary steps to eradicate the sow thistle. I think the work could be done under a thousand dollars, and it seems to me the Dominion government should be prepared to spend this sum to do away with the nuisance on their own 'and. I will take the opportunity of discussing the matter with the miinster in his office some day and I think possibly I may be able to suggest to him a way in which this difficulty can be overcome. I would ask his support for the proposal I make.
Does my hon, friend suggest that the people in his constituency have discovered a means of eradicating sow thistle?

One method recommended by the provincial department of agriculture was covering the patch of sow thistle with tar paper for a year or two. That would smother the weeds.
Mr. MOTHERWELL': We will do our best in the matter.

I should like the minister to direct his attention to the question which has been touched upon by my hon. friend (Mr. Coote). This parliament has jurisdiction over agriculture to a limited extent, and the provinces also exercise jurisdiction in this respect. The minister was at one time Minister of Agriculture in the province from which he comes and he now holds a similar portfolio in the federal government. Now my observation is this, that vast sums of money are voted here which would accomplish much greater
IMr. Motherwell.!
results if their expenditure were more or less directed by the local authorities. In most matters centralization has failed, and any endeavour to standardize agriculture must necessarily fail in Canada as it has done elsewhere. My hon. friend from Macleod has discussed a matter to which I was going to refer. The Dominion government owns large areas of land in western Canada: it has Indian reserves, bird sanctuaries, forest reserves and other lands, some of which are occupied while others are vacant. Surely when the provincial authorities are endeavouring to deal with weeds and various other problems incident to agriculture, and are confronted with the difficulty of lands owned by the Dominion not being cared for, it is obvious that the entire effort is lost. The Quill lake reserve, to which the minister has referred, is a striking illustration of the point I desire to make. Of what value is it to spend federal money to bring about the results which the minister so earnestly desires if the provinces, in their efforts, find themselves absolutely unable to approach federally-owned lands, and if thistles and noxious weeds of various kinds flourish, with the result that the whole district is destroyed? Of what use is the expenditure of federal money when the federal government has not done its duty in relation to these lands? That is the position with respect to some Indian reserves in Alberta, and this is true also of other federally owned lands. I think the minister would be doing a great, service to the country if, in his approach to the problems with which he has to cope, he regarded his duties as Minister of Agriculture as being of a national character, and correlated the efforts of his department with those of the departments of agriculture in the various provinces. The department of agriculture in Quebec, for example, has to deal with problems entirely different from those that face the department of agriculture in Alberta; and where you have federally owned lands in the western provinces in connection with which there are all the difficulties to which the minister has made reference, how can we hope to eradicate any pest from a district adjacent to such lands if the federal government does not devote its attention to the territory under its jurisdiction? That is a real, live problem. Farmers have spoken to me about it and I know that the provincial authorities have from time to time come right up against it. I myself have seen, travelling over the country in automobiles, and sometimes within the right of way of the railways, large areas of noxious weeds, seeds being disseminated over the surrounding soil; and the pest has persisted notwithstanding the best efforts of the provincial authorities, simply because the federal government has not
Supply-Agriculture

discharged its responsibility with respect to its own. property or to those matters over which it exercises sole control.
I submit that the function of the federal department of agriculture is in a large sense national. It never was intended that the department should undertake detailed operations affecting agriculture in the provinces, and even though it makes grants in aid of work that may be done by the provinces, with assistance from the Dominion, the federal department should not engage in these small activities which I have mentioned, if they fail to look after their own property, with resultant injury to the work done by the provinces, especially in the west. I do not expect the minister to express an opinion at the moment, but I should like him to consider the problem that confronts the department of agriculture from the standpoint of a greater degree of decentralization, and an increased effort to discharge the broad national duties that rest upon the department in the matter of pure seed.
With regard to other .matters to which the minister has alluded, it is perfectly clear that this department should exercise jurisdiction. But when it comes to the question of inspection and matters of a kindred nature, there is the danger that a situation may arise similar to that which was created with respect to eggs. The courts will declare that the legislation is invalid because it interferes with civil property rights .within the jurisdiction of the provinces. My observation leads me to the conclusion that an effort is being made by the federal Department of Agriculture to pay too much attention to work that really constitutes an interference with the industry, at the expense of the local authorities who are more competent and are better able to deal with the situation. And this apart from the first point I made, namely, the failure of the federal government to discharge its duties with respect to federally owned property, with resultant danger, indeed injury, to adjoining lands, whether privately or publicly owned.

I do not want my
hon. friend's remarks to pass without consideration. I thank him for the suggestions he has offered. I would point out, however, that there are some things which cannot be helped-My hon. friend (Mr. Manion) is sitting opposite, and as a medical man he knows that so far no cure has been found for cancer. Are you going to reprove or to hold up to ridicule the whole medical fraternity because such a cure has not yet been discovered? If any farmer who is familiar with the sow thistle can suggest a recipe for eradicating it where it is found in low-lying soil, wet enough 
to encourage its growth and not dry enough to plough, then it seems to me his fortune is made. I do not mind admitting that I have no remedy to offer. Just as the medical man knows that there is no cure for cancer, so I do not pretend to be able to do the impossible.
I did not suggest that.

There is no reason, however, why we should not persist in our efforts to find some means of eradicating the pest. The problem is a serious one which I have been studying ever since coming here, as indeed I did in Regina. The sow thistle develops in cultivated land more rapidly than elsewhere. The farmers, of course, like to pass the buck to the government, but this matter can be dealt with only by cooperation. The farmers will say, "What is the use of our cleaning up so long as the Dominion Government's lands are polluted?" And I presume the federal officials will take a similar attitude. Everyone knows that the pest exists and we can only be thankful that but seventy-five per cent of it is fertile.
With regard to the overlapping, that question came up at the interprovincial conference, and it must be admitted that there was a good deal of overlapping many years ago. The Hon. Mr. Hoadley brought that question up, and after it was discussed everyone agreed that very substantial progress was being made both by the federal government and by the provinces in cutting out the overlapping.
Perhaps the minister did not hear me; I was speaking with respect to federal property.
There was another matter which I took no chance of forgetting; that is, interference with agriculture.
No, no.

Yes, I remember
that. My hon. friend said there was a great tendency on the part of the government to interfere with agriculture, and I think my hon. friend referred to the standardization of products both for export and for home consumption. Of course you have to interfere, but we never interfere until there is a reasonably strong sentiment in the community for the action we propose. Invariably we start with a voluntary system, as we did in the grading of cheese and butter, until about three-quarters of the people concerned are carrying it out. Then it is made compulsory, so there is no unnecessary interference. Ask any of the members from the maritime provinces if there is any unnecessary interfer-

Supply-Agriculture
ence now with their grading. We do not perform these services until we have a strong . public sentiment behind us; there would be absolutely no use doing these things in any other way. If my hon. friend were as familiar with this work as he is with the practice of law he would realize that you cannot do this work without some interference any more than you can make omelettes without breaking eggs.

My hon. friend has misunderstood me. I was not talking about interference in that sense; I was talking about the federal power as distinguished from the provincial power, and I asked whether my hon. friend did not think the federal Department of Agriculture should at least see to it that federally owned lands observe the law with respect to noxious weeds, rather than have them as pest centres in communities which are otherwise free.
I will take that up with the Minister of the Interior.

You could spend the entire revenue of the Dominion of Canada trying to clear up the federal lands, and my hon. friend the leader of the opposition knows that. In western Canada years ago lands were opened up which never should have been touched, and now these have been abandoned. They are located all over the prairie provinces; they are covered with weeds, and you could not possibly clear them up. In the case mentioned by my hon. friend (Mr. Coote), probably that is a little plot of land owned by the government which could be easily cleaned up by the people of that town, but if you try to clear up every abandoned homestead and pre-emption in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, together with the road allowances and all the landis belonging to the Dominion government, you could spend the whole revenue of this country in one year.

And then not
accomplish your purpose.

As I said before, I did not
want to delay this item, but I must reply very briefly to the remarks of the minister. In this particular case I have heard the weeds were started through the practice of some person or some firm in the town of Macleod of throwing on this vacant property straw which had come in a packing case. Sow thistle appeared where these people were in the habit of doing that, and it has spread from that Dominion-owned land to the district surrounding. I do not want to be misunderstood when I say this piece of property could be taken care of very easily; it is not very large and could be cleaned right up. It is larger than it was two years ago, of course, but even now it could be dug out by the roots, and in a few years the good done by removing that source of contagion would amount to thousands of dollars. The only two patches of sow thistle which amount to anything in my constituency, so far as I know, are or Dominion-owned lands; one is on an Indiar reserve and the other on this property in the town of Macleod. The superintendent o1 Indian Affairs is doing his best to look aftei the sow thistle on the Indian reserve, and I thank him for it. I believe it is being dug out by the roots, and I think the same should be done in connection with this property in Macleod.

I am inclined
to think that this whole discussion is slightly put of order; sow thistle does not come under this item at all. It may be true, as the leader of the opposition has said, that a good deal of government land in covered with sow thistle and other weeds, but the Department of the Interior is ready at all times to cooperate with the local authorities in controlling these weeds. There are places where that is very difficult to do, but in regard to the land in Macleod I believe my hon. friend would find the Department of the Interior willing to turn over that land to the town for public use, and the town could clean it up. It is only reasonable that that should be done; the town was responsible for the pollution and they should clean it up. I believe that to be the practice of the department everywhere, and why it is being dis-. cussed under this item is more than I can imagine.

Item agreed to.
For experiments in dehydration of fruits and vegetables, $10,000.

I should like to ask the
minister for the total amount spent to date in carrying out these experiments, in what districts throughout Canada the experiments have been carried on, and the varieties of fruit dealt with.

We have had three experimental dehydrating plants, one at the central farm at Ottawa, one at Grimsby and another at Penticton; we have had very good results, and a number of private commercial enterprises have sprung up. I believe some of these are located at Vernon and Kelowna, and are doing very well. We import enor-

Supply-Agriculture
mous quantities of dehydrated fruit, and we can very well supply a great deal of that quantity ourselves, but for some reason or other this has not been done, which is one reason why the department has spent a certain amount of money in developing these plants. We have a dehydrating committee in charge of this work, consisting of Mr. E. S. Archibald, B.A., Director of Experimental Farms, chairman; George E. McIntosh. Dominion Fruit Commissioner; F. T. Shutt, M.A., Dominion Chemist; W. T. Macoun, Dominion Horticulturist, and C. S. McGill-ivray, Chief Canning Inspector. A number of these gentlemen have been overseas attending a research conference, and Mr. Archibald has just returned from attending a dairy conference in the west. They have not had an opportunity, therefore, to lay out a program for this winter, and unless something more advantageous turns up we expect to go through with the same program. My friends from the maritime provinces will be interested to learn that a number of gentlemen came here from Berwick in Kings to see what could be done and if any assistance could be obtained in the establishment of a plant of this kind. Our vote was exhausted at the time, however, so we could not give them any money, but we put them in touch with a competent engineer and gave them all the information we had. Like many other enterprises they did not have sufficient funds, and their plant was not as successful as they would have liked, because they were unable to put in proper insulation, with the result that it did not do as well as they expected. We have it in mind to assist that plant and to help put it on its feet with this grant. The dehydration committee has a number of proposals before it. They did well down there but suffered from a lack of money. They did not have quite enough capital to operate the plant and we did not have any money at that time to assist them.
What has been the amount expended in carrying out these experiments?

Fruits that have
been dehydrated are: apples, apricots, blackberries, blueberries, crabapples, cherries, raspberries, strawberries, gooseberries, loganberries, peaches, pears and plums; and vegetables. I think the process is going to be quite successful.

The minister has not
answered my question as to what amount has been expended in carrying out these experiments.

The house at first voted $15,000 and we have not exceeded the appropriation. This is the fourth year for the work, and the amount now asked for is $10,000'. We have no idea, I think, of extending the system to tire Okanagan valley. There are two very good plants in British Columbia, one at Vernon and the other at Kelowna, but I have not visited them since they were established. I shoidd like to see a similar plant established in the Annapolis valley. They did start a commercial plant there but through lack of capital it is not as successful as it should have been, and I feel we might possibly help them out in the matter of a proper dehydrating equipment or something of the kind, so as to help them to get on their feet.

In the Fraser valley we have looked for something in the line of experiments on the part of the department in the dehydration and crystallization of fruit. A large quantity of dehj'drated and crytallized fruit is being imported into the country at the present time, whereas tons of fresh fruit are going to waste in the fruit districts of the Fraser valley. We believe that such fruits as loganberries, raspberries, strawberries, cherries and peaches could be handled if we had some process of dehydration or crystallization. The minister has referred to commercial plants that have failed. We have had commercial plants start in the district referred to and they have failed also. I understood that the object of this vote was to develop some process by which a dehydration industry could take care of the fruit and produce of our growers which otherwise would be wasted. To-day tons of fruit are being wasted which could be utilized if we had some process for the dehydration and crystallization of fruits.
Mr. MOTHERWELL; We shall be glad to look into the matter of crystallization. My hon. friend agrees that there is no further necessity to experiment in the matter of the dehydration of fruit on the Pacific. It is the crystallization that he is speaking of now, is it not?

I do not think there have
been any experiments in the dehydration of the small fruits.
Oh, yes.

Not in the lower Fraser district. I have been trying for two years to get some information from the department for people in that district and I have been unable to obtain it. All the information given

Supply-Agriculture
in the departmental report is that experiments in the dehydration of fruits and vegetables have been continued. -

The department
recently got out a publication-I do not think my hon. friend's attention has been drawn to it-giving a summary of four years' work by the dehydration committee. The program for the coming year has not yet been outlined by the committee owing to some of them not having returned to Canada until quite recently.

I should like to get some
information from the minister. I do not speak disparagingly of the vote because I quite realize that some aid or encouragement is necessary to start this industry in order that it may be opened to the fruit growing districts of the province of Nova Scotia. He stated that some portion of the $10,000 in this vote is to go to a commercial enterprise in Berwick. Could the minister inform the house just what proportion of the $10,000 is to be granted to that enterprise, and will he disclose its name?
We have a right to know it.
I think the information is due to the house. I ask only for the purpose of information. .
The representatives of the company came up to see us about two years ago.
Which company?

I have no recollection of the name of the company, I have never had an opportunity of discussing it with the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley). However, I do not recall the name of the company.
It is not the Apple Crisp Company, is it?

I do not know. I think it would take the whole of this vote for the improvement of plants already established once you began installing better equipment and providing cork insulation. Those improvements would soon eat up the $10,000.

If some portion of this vote of $10,000 is to be used to assist private enterprise, no matter how laudable, I should like the minister to take the house into his confidence and inform us what enterprise it is.
We have a right to know.

I do not care to act without the advice of the dehydration committee, the members of which have returned to Canada only recently. I would not care to give a straight pledge that the money would be invested there or somewhere else.
If my hon. friend thinks he is not being given sufficient information we will strike the vote out.

I am not asking that the
vote be struck out; I merely want to get information before the vote passes. If the minister cannot supply the information I suggest that, he let the item stand and perhaps he will be in a position to give it to us to-morrow.

We have not the information my hon. friend would like to have, and that I would like to have. We have always been governed by the representations of the dehydrating committee, but my sympathies are in the direction of helping out the commercial plant that was started, but which, partly for want of capital, failed.
What plant is it?

I only want to see that the money which is given for dehydration purposes in the maritime provinces is going to do some real good. I do not object to a vote for dehydration, but I should like to have an assurance that this money will be spent where it will do the most good. I want something done to benefit the industry.

Perhaps it would
have been better if I had not mentioned that institution when I did not know the name of it.
The hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) is present. He can speak for his constituency.

Is the minister asking
parliament to vote money when he does not know what he is going to do with it?

I think I have
explained for at least the third time why I have not the information. The dehydration committee were not all in Ottawa until yesterday, and I should like to be advised by them because they have a knowledge of the work. If it is a technical violation of the rights of parliament not to have all this information, even for the reasons I have given, I shall be delighted, in order to bring myself in line with the rights of parliament, to move that this vote be struck out. Let it be remembered that I do this not in any spirit of petulance but because I recognize that the criticism is right. I think, however, the circumstances ought to be sufficiently
Supply-Agriculture

extenuating and the amount is so small that my hon. friend should not hang on to it in that way like a pup on a roof.

While the minister's application may fit, it was because I have had some experience in connection with governmental expenditures in the maritime provinces that I drew the attention of the committee to this vote. I was only asking for information and I am surprised that the minister cannot furnish it,

In view of the
high regard in which I hold the maritime provinces I should not like to see the vote struck out, but I admit that the circumstances to which I have referred render it impossible for me to give the information asked for. The committee can take the item as it is or let it go out.
This parliament has not yet come to that.

The item can stand and
we can get the information later.

The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) has rather invited me to speak about this, and my statement will be very brief. I never knew, until I heard the minister so state, that any firm in Berwick, which is in my constituency, had applied for a grant, and I do not know now what firm it is.

I do not know
where it is except that it is in the Annapolis valley.

I have not the slightest idea what company or firm has applied for this grant. If the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg, who has had such an unfavourable experience in connection with governmental expenditures, is the least bit worried that the money is going in a wrong direction, he can rest assured that, so far as I know, it is not going to any friends of mine. I think it would be a shame to cut out this item. This experimental work should be assisted and extended, and if anything of this sort can be done in the Annapolis valley, it should certainly be done. I wanted to speak simply to obviate the impression that was left by the hon. member on the other side of the house that some unwise or unnecessary expenditure was contemplated in the Annapolis valley.

May I suggest to the
minister that the suggestion of the hon. member behind me that the item should stand seems a reasonable one? Parliament is not going to prorogue to-morrow, and we have plenty of time.
[Mr. Motherwell.3

All right, we will let it stand. The committee can see how amiable the minister is to-night.
Item stands.
Live stock, including grants to exhibitions feeder shows, etc., $1,480,000.

I have been requested by an hon. member to let this item stand because he would like to get some information on it.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

subtopic: CHANGE OF ORDER OF REFERENCE FROM RAILWAY COMMITTEE TO MISCELLANEOUS PRIVATE BILLS COMMITTEE

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CHANGE OF ORDER OF REFERENCE FROM RAILWAY COMMITTEE TO MISCELLANEOUS PRIVATE BILLS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last
three bills dealing with the incorporation of a memorial bridge company, a transit company, and a gorge bridge company, were before the house for second reading. They were being referred to the select standing committee on miscellaneous private bills when I directed attention to the fact that they dealt with railways and the construction of a bridge and should, therefore, be referred to the railway committee. I am now advised that such bills usually go in the first instance to the select standing committee on miscellaneous private bills and if it is thought desirable they may be sent afterwards to the railway committee. I therefore move:
That the order of the house of Friday, February 10, referring the following private bills to the select standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, be discharged, and that the said bills he referred to the select standing committee on miscellaneous private bills, namely,-
Bill No. 14, to incorporate the Niagara Falls Memorial Bridge Company.
Bill No. 23, to incorporate St. Clair Transit Company.
Bill No. 25, to incorporate Niagara Gorge Bridge Company.
That puts the matter where it was originally. On Friday the Solicitor General, following my comment, mentioned that last year a similar bill had been referred to the committee on miscellaneous private bills.

subtopic: CHANGE OF ORDER OF REFERENCE FROM RAILWAY COMMITTEE TO MISCELLANEOUS PRIVATE BILLS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I mentioned it.

Motion agreed to.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.

Earl of Oxford and Asquith
Wednesday, February 15, 1928
